articles.title: This is my new favorite laptop, but thanks to RAMageddon the price already went up by $800
articles.summary: The Framework Laptop 13 Pro is a repairable and upgradeable notebook with modular ports and MacBook Pro-level build quality. It also has a high price thanks to RAMageddon.
articles.body: Framework laptops always come with compromises in exchange for their unique DIY premise. Even though you pay extra for one compared to sleeker options from competitors, it’s easier to excuse minor flaws for modular ports, easy repairs, and an impressive range of upgradeable parts. So what happens when Framework goes “Pro”? We get a one-of-a-kind jewel among notebooks. The 13 Pro corrects and improves many shortcomings of the regular Laptop 13. It has a bright and sharp touchscreen, the best haptic trackpad not made by Apple, and an impeccable build and feel. Take all that and marry it to a great Intel chip and cutting-edge user-replaceable LPCAMM2 memory — both of which help to better balance performance and extra-long battery life — and you’ve got something really special. But what if this all happens in the throes of RAMageddon, with ever-increasing tech prices? Well, it’s now expensive as hell, of course. Our higher-end prebuilt review unit of the Laptop 13 Pro with a Windows license was meant to cost $2,299 when it arrived at my door, but after fresh memory price increases it’s now a nausea-inducing $3,099. An $800 price increase before reaching a single customer. We’ve seen lots of recent sticker shock, but this one especially hurts. [Product: Framework Laptop 13 Pro (Intel Core Ultra X7 358H) | https://framework.pxf.io/c/482924/1459308/17284?u=https%3A%2F%2Fframe.work%2Fproducts%2Flaptop13pro-intel-ultra-3%2Fconfiguration%2Fnew] --- Component report card * Screen: B * Webcam: B * Keyboard: A * Trackpad: A * Port selection: A * Speakers: C * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 1 on the Windows prebuilt (but only on the bottom) --- The Laptop 13 Pro is an all-black machine with an exquisite matte finish. It actually looks black instead of some variation of dark gray, and it feels rigid and well crafted — far from the hodgepodge erector set of its bigger cousin, the Laptop 16, or the good but slightly lower-quality build of the standard Laptop 13. Inside the 13 Pro are new Intel Panther Lake chips with LPCAMM2 RAM, or it can be optioned with last-gen AMD processors and slower SODIMM DDR5 memory. Our prebuilt review unit has a 16-core Intel Core Ultra X7 358H CPU with a 12-core Arc B390 integrated GPU, 32GB of RAM, 1TB SSD, and four modular USB-C ports. Unlike other Frameworks, each port supports Thunderbolt 4, DisplayPort 2.1, and up to 140W charging so you can freely mount your modular expansion cards without any restrictions. Everything here is really well put together. There’s no flex or give to the chassis or keyboard deck, even though everything’s easily disassembled with a handful of simple screws. The keyboard itself is great to type on. It maintains the nice 1.5mm key travel and tactility of the regular Laptop 13, but feels ever-so-slightly better thanks to a new one-piece aluminum frame. The 1080p webcam is a holdover from the regular model, maintaining its solid performance — it’s pretty sharp, if just a touch grainy in some lighting. The big upgrades to the 13 Pro’s components are the new haptic trackpad and touchscreen LCD. This is the best non-Apple haptic trackpad I’ve ever used. It’s very responsive to “clicks” from corner to corner, and it feels and sounds just right. The new screen is still a 13.5-inch matte-finish 120Hz IPS panel with 2880 x 1920 resolution for that excellent 3:2 aspect ratio, but it’s brighter (700 nits) and touch-enabled. Until now, a touchscreen on a Framework was only found on the cheaper Laptop 12. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The 13 Pro’s audio comes from a pair of side-firing stereo speakers. The speakers were one of the weaker points of the standard Laptop 13, and they’re the 13 Pro’s biggest fault. The side-mounted orientation creates a tiny bit of a soundstage, but overall the speakers sound a little thin and treble-y with minimal bass. When I reviewed the Laptop 13, a savvy commenter pointed me toward open-source app FxSound to help with its audio woes. FxSound does help the 13 Pro sound noticeably better and fuller (with lots of EQ and boost options), but unfortunately for Linux users it’s Windows only. The Intel chip and LPCAMM2 memory inside do a great job delivering on both performance and exceptional power efficiency. This newer style of compression-mounted memory is better for both of those factors, just like LPDDR5X, but without having to be soldered to the main board. The tradeoff for using LPCAMM2 is that it’s newer tech that’s generally pricier than DDR5 (gulp). [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0015.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0017.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0018.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0019.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0020.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0021.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Thanks to this memory and the power sipping of Intel’s Panther Lake chip, the Laptop 13 Pro is a battery champ. Framework claims it lasts up to 17 hours during active web usage, but that’s with brightness at only 250 nits. Even at 80 to 100 percent brightness and keeping over a dozen Chrome tabs plus Slack and Signal open while occasionally streaming Apple Music, it took me around 10.5 hours to go from fully charged to 12 percent battery left in the tank. Compared to the Laptop 13’s AMD chip, the 13 Pro is outstanding. Raw performance from the Ultra X7 358H is good too. While Framework bills the Laptop 13 Pro as “the MacBook Pro for Linux users,” it still doesn’t quite keep up with Apple’s much cheaper laptops. (At least on Windows. I’ll have to see about testing it on Linux in a potential follow-up like I did the Framework Desktop.) It’s not left in the dust, however, especially in graphics-heavy tasks like Blender. That’s where the 12-core integrated GPU, a major improvement over the regular Framework 13, shines brightest. I was slightly taken aback by its low scoring in the PugetBench test for Adobe Premiere, and I expected slightly faster rendering in our Premiere 4K export test (see our benchmark table below), but real-world usage hasn’t disappointed. I was quite happy with how the 13 Pro handled Adobe Lightroom Classic. It took just over seven minutes to import a card full of nearly 2,000 66-megapixel RAW images (93GB of files), and about that long to render all the initial previews. It also performed well when bouncing around a large selection of those images and making various edits. I know firsthand that even a base M5 MacBook Pro is faster at this kind of stuff, but the Framework performed just fine. While the Framework isn’t built specifically for gaming, running Windows 11 immediately gives it that strength over any Mac by default. And the 13 Pro’s potent integrated graphics are just fine for 1080p gaming at low to even medium settings — typically delivering 50 to 60fps on titles like Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Helldivers 2 when using Intel’s XeSS upscaling. It could even push to the panel’s full 2880 x 1920 resolution in Cyberpunk and use frame generation to maintain 60fps (natively rendering 30fps, which is fine for a single-player game like that). [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0040.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0044.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0042.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0049.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] This laptop does get hot under load or when playing demanding games. The chassis is about the same thickness as a 14-inch MacBook Pro, though a touch lighter, and it can feel like it’s going to light your lap on fire when under full load. Your fingers thankfully don’t get toasted on the keyboard in either the home row or WASD positions, but just beyond that, near the hinge, I measured it briefly hitting 57 degrees Celsius / 135 degrees Fahrenheit. It didn’t stay that hot for long, but thermals might be a slight concern for people looking to work this laptop hard for lengthy periods. As nice as the Laptop 13 Pro is, there’s no escaping its new astronomical price and the turmoil surrounding its launch. Framework has raised prices on all of its devices, and the 13 Pro isn’t being spared even before its launch. Just last week, Framework bumped some reserved preorders down from 32GB of RAM to 16GB and raised the price of new preorders by as much as $800. Browsing the Framework subreddit and seeing even the brand’s most hardcore fans saying they’re being priced out and canceling their orders feels grim. We’re already seeing other tech companies cancel devices or give up entirely on some markets because of skyrocketing RAMageddon prices, and the fear is how it might affect the long-term viability of niche tech products like Framework’s. The slightly good news is that if existing Framework Laptop 13 owners like what the 13 Pro is offering, they can buy many of those parts a la carte and upgrade to the specific components they care most about — from the Intel mainboard with LPCAMM2 to the brighter touchscreen and haptic trackpad. That doesn’t make those upgrades cheap, but it beats buying a whole new laptop. And thus we’ve arrived at the whole point of Framework in the first place. Non-upgradeable laptops like the MacBook Pro may be the “better” buy for performance per dollar (even after Apple’s own price increases), but those computers always remain whatever configuration you bought on day one. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0024.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0025.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0026.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0027.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0028.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0029.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0030.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0032.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0034.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0033.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0035.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0036.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] It’s hard not to love Framework laptops. (The hardware, specifically. The actual company is easier to have mixed feelings about.) The 13 Pro is the most complete Framework laptop yet — the one with the fewest faults to overlook in favor of all its cool and nifty DIY features. It’d be a great overall package even without upgradeability, those awesome modular ports, and easy repairability. Factor all that in and it’s one of my favorite laptops I’ve ever used. But then I look at the price. Like other recent laptops I’ve reviewed, I’m left wondering what could have been if RAMageddon never happened. While I’d love to entertain the dream of the 13 Pro one day coming down in price after this storm is weathered, there’s no safe harbor yet in sight. --- Framework Laptop 13 Pro specs (as reviewed) * Display: 13.5-inch (2880 x 1920) 30-120Hz IPS touchscreen * CPU: Intel Core Ultra X7 358H * GPU: Intel Arc B390 * RAM: 32GB LPCAMM2 * Storage: 1TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe * Webcam: 1080p 30fps with privacy switches (mic and camera) * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 * Ports: 4x modular USB-C / Thunderbolt 4 ports for Framework Expansion Cards * Biometrics: fingerprint sensor in power button * Weight: 3.17 pounds / 1.44kg * Dimensions: 0.62 x 11.68 x 9.01 inches / 15.85 x 296.63 x 228.98mm * Battery: 74.45Wh * Price: $3,099 (with $200 Windows 11 Pro license) --- Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

Unlike other Frameworks, each port supports Thunderbolt 4, DisplayPort 2.1, and up to 140W charging so you can freely mount your modular expansion cards without any restrictions. Everything here is really well put together. There’s no flex or give to the chassis or keyboard deck, even though everything’s easily disassembled with a handful of simple screws. The keyboard itself is great to type on. It maintains the nice 1.5mm key travel and tactility of the regular Laptop 13, but feels ever-so-slightly better thanks to a new one-piece aluminum frame. The 1080p webcam is a holdover from the regular model, maintaining its solid performance — it’s pretty sharp, if just a touch grainy in some lighting. The big upgrades to the 13 Pro’s components are the new haptic trackpad and touchscreen LCD. This is the best non-Apple haptic trackpad I’ve ever used. It’s very responsive to “clicks” from corner to corner, and it feels and sounds just right. The new screen is still a 13.5-inch matte-finish 120Hz IPS panel with 2880 x 1920 resolution for that excellent 3:2 aspect ratio, but it’s brighter (700 nits) and touch-enabled. Until now, a touchscreen on a Framework was only found on the cheaper Laptop 12. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0008.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The 13 Pro’s audio comes from a pair of side-firing stereo speakers. The speakers were one of the weaker points of the standard Laptop 13, and they’re the 13 Pro’s biggest fault. The side-mounted orientation creates a tiny bit of a soundstage, but overall the speakers sound a little thin and treble-y with minimal bass. When I reviewed the Laptop 13, a savvy commenter pointed me toward open-source app FxSound to help with its audio woes. FxSound does help the 13 Pro sound noticeably better and fuller (with lots of EQ and boost options), but unfortunately for Linux users it’s Windows only. The Intel chip and LPCAMM2 memory inside do a great job delivering on both performance and exceptional power efficiency. This newer style of compression-mounted memory is better for both of those factors, just like LPDDR5X, but without having to be soldered to the main board. The tradeoff for using LPCAMM2 is that it’s newer tech that’s generally pricier than DDR5 (gulp). [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0015.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0017.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0018.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0019.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0020.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0021.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Thanks to this memory and the power sipping of Intel’s Panther Lake chip, the Laptop 13 Pro is a battery champ. Framework claims it lasts up to 17 hours during active web usage, but that’s with brightness at only 250 nits. Even at 80 to 100 percent brightness and keeping over a dozen Chrome tabs plus Slack and Signal open while occasionally streaming Apple Music, it took me around 10.5 hours to go from fully charged to 12 percent battery left in the tank. Compared to the Laptop 13’s AMD chip, the 13 Pro is outstanding. Raw performance from the Ultra X7 358H is good too. While Framework bills the Laptop 13 Pro as “the MacBook Pro for Linux users,” it still doesn’t quite keep up with Apple’s much cheaper laptops. (At least on Windows. I’ll have to see about testing it on Linux in a potential follow-up like I did the Framework Desktop.) It’s not left in the dust, however, especially in graphics-heavy tasks like Blender. That’s where the 12-core integrated GPU, a major improvement over the regular Framework 13, shines brightest. I was slightly taken aback by its low scoring in the PugetBench test for Adobe Premiere, and I expected slightly faster rendering in our Premiere 4K export test (see our benchmark table below), but real-world usage hasn’t disappointed. I was quite happy with how the 13 Pro handled Adobe Lightroom Classic. It took just over seven minutes to import a card full of nearly 2,000 66-megapixel RAW images (93GB of files), and about that long to render all the initial previews. It also performed well when bouncing around a large selection of those images and making various edits. I know firsthand that even a base M5 MacBook Pro is faster at this kind of stuff, but the Framework performed just fine. While the Framework isn’t built specifically for gaming, running Windows 11 immediately gives it that strength over any Mac by default. And the 13 Pro’s potent integrated graphics are just fine for 1080p gaming at low to even medium settings — typically delivering 50 to 60fps on titles like Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Helldivers 2 when using Intel’s XeSS upscaling. It could even push to the panel’s full 2880 x 1920 resolution in Cyberpunk and use frame generation to maintain 60fps (natively rendering 30fps, which is fine for a single-player game like that). [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0040.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0044.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0042.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0049.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] This laptop does get hot under load or when playing demanding games. The chassis is about the same thickness as a 14-inch MacBook Pro, though a touch lighter, and it can feel like it’s going to light your lap on fire when under full load. Your fingers thankfully don’t get toasted on the keyboard in either the home row or WASD positions, but just beyond that, near the hinge, I measured it briefly hitting 57 degrees Celsius / 135 degrees Fahrenheit. It didn’t stay that hot for long, but thermals might be a slight concern for people looking to work this laptop hard for lengthy periods. As nice as the Laptop 13 Pro is, there’s no escaping its new astronomical price and the turmoil surrounding its launch. Framework has raised prices on all of its devices, and the 13 Pro isn’t being spared even before its launch. Just last week, Framework bumped some reserved preorders down from 32GB of RAM to 16GB and raised the price of new preorders by as much as $800. Browsing the Framework subreddit and seeing even the brand’s most hardcore fans saying they’re being priced out and canceling their orders feels grim. We’re already seeing other tech companies cancel devices or give up entirely on some markets because of skyrocketing RAMageddon prices, and the fear is how it might affect the long-term viability of niche tech products like Framework’s. The slightly good news is that if existing Framework Laptop 13 owners like what the 13 Pro is offering, they can buy many of those parts a la carte and upgrade to the specific components they care most about — from the Intel mainboard with LPCAMM2 to the brighter touchscreen and haptic trackpad. That doesn’t make those upgrades cheap, but it beats buying a whole new laptop. And thus we’ve arrived at the whole point of Framework in the first place. Non-upgradeable laptops like the MacBook Pro may be the “better” buy for performance per dollar (even after Apple’s own price increases), but those computers always remain whatever configuration you bought on day one. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0024.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0025.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0029.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0030.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0031.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0032.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0034.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0033.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0035.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268670_Framework_Laptop_13_Pro_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0036.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] It’s hard not to love Framework laptops. (The hardware, specifically. The actual company is easier to have mixed feelings about.) The 13 Pro is the most complete Framework laptop yet — the one with the fewest faults to overlook in favor of all its cool and nifty DIY features. It’d be a great overall package even without upgradeability, those awesome modular ports, and easy repairability. Factor all that in and it’s one of my favorite laptops I’ve ever used. But then I look at the price. Like other recent laptops I’ve reviewed, I’m left wondering what could have been if RAMageddon never happened. While I’d love to entertain the dream of the 13 Pro one day coming down in price after this storm is weathered, there’s no safe harbor yet in sight. --- Framework Laptop 13 Pro specs (as reviewed) * Display: 13.5-inch (2880 x 1920) 30-120Hz IPS touchscreen * CPU: Intel Core Ultra X7 358H * GPU: Intel Arc B390 * RAM: 32GB LPCAMM2 * Storage: 1TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe * Webcam: 1080p 30fps with privacy switches (mic and camera) * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6 * Ports: 4x modular USB-C / Thunderbolt 4 ports for Framework Expansion Cards * Biometrics: fingerprint sensor in power button * Weight: 3.17 pounds / 1.44kg * Dimensions: 0.62 x 11.68 x 9.01 inches / 15.85 x 296.63 x 228.98mm * Battery: 74.45Wh * Price: $3,099 (with $200 Windows 11 Pro license) --- Photography by Antonio G. articles.title: Apple launches 'Upgrade' device leasing program in partnership with Klarna | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The rollout of the program comes as Apple has been struggling with supply chain issues related to "RAMageddon," which refers to the industry-wide shortage of memory chips that is driving up the price of hardware.
articles.body:
Apple is introducing a new leasing program in partnership with the “buy now, pay later” service Klarna, giving eligible customers the option to pay for Apple devices through monthly installments, the tech giant announced on Tuesday. The program is available for the iPhone, Apple Watch, Mac, and iPad on the Apple Store online, in the Apple Store app, and at Apple Store locations in the United States.

Leasing prices start at $17.99 per month for iPhone, $11.99 per month for Apple Watch, $24.99 per month for Mac, and $11.99 per month for iPad. Apple Upgrade offers one- and two-year leasing options for iPhone and Apple Watch, and two- and three-year options for Mac and iPad.

At the end of the lease term, customers can upgrade to the latest generation of their device, purchase their current device with a one-time payment, or return it and exit the program, Apple says.

The rollout of the program comes as Apple has been struggling with supply chain issues related to “RAMageddon,” which refers to the industry-wide shortage of memory chips that is driving up the price of hardware. As a result, Apple recently announced price hikes for its Mac and iPad lineups, sparing the iPhone for now. The new Upgrade program seems to be Apple’s answer to making those higher prices more manageable for consumers.

Customers can manage their lease directly in the Klarna app, where they can view their billing schedule and track remaining payments.

With the launch of the new Upgrade program, Apple is discontinuing its existing in-house financing and installment programs in the U.S., which include the iPhone Upgrade Program and iPhone Payments.

The official launch follows a report from Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman last week, which revealed that Apple was preparing to introduce a lease-to-own program for its devices.

Apple says that when customers enroll in Apple Upgrade, they can lower their monthly lease payments by trading in their existing device through its Apple Trade In program. They can also earn 3% Daily Cash back when using Apple Card to make their lease payments.

articles.title: Apple stockpiles inventory as it braces for 'significant supply constraints' | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple is worried enough about supply shortages that it reported about $11.1 billion in inventory, which is almost double the $5.7 billion it reported last September.
articles.body:
As the generative AI boom drives steep demand for hardware components, Apple and other hardware makers are facing what outgoing CEO Tim Cook calls “a hundred-year flood [on] memory pricing,” which is severely impacting the cost of producing iPhones, MacBooks, and other devices.

Apple described its recent earnings report as its “strongest June quarter ever,” with iPhone and Mac sales performing better than expected, growing 22% and 29%, respectively, year-over-year. Yet the company is bracing for memory shortages, known as RAMageddon , to get even worse. Apple’s biggest challenge is securing the advanced memory nodes used in its Apple silicon chips, which power the A-Series and M-Series processors used in iPhones and Macs.

“We continue to expect high levels of demand. However, with less flexibility in supply chain, we expect the impact from the supply constraints to increase significantly sequentially,” Cook said on Apple’s quarterly earnings call. “We’re seeing some very significant constraints currently with limited flexibility in the supply chain to remedy it.”

Apple is evidently worried enough about supply shortages that it reported $11.1 billion in inventory, nearly double the $5.7 billion it reported last September. This marks a break from Cook’s long-held supply chain approach, which has emphasized minimizing how much inventory Apple has on hand.

These constraints led Apple to “reluctantly” raise the price of Macs and iPads last month, Cook added. Other companies that have raised hardware prices include Meta , Samsung , Microsoft , and Sony .

“We’re going to be scrambling on the supply side, essentially,” Cook said.

For the upcoming quarter, Apple is predicting revenue growth between 9% and 11% year-over-year. But in the last several quarters, Apple has maintained about 16% year-over-year growth. Of course, that worries investors — Apple stock dropped 6% in after-hours trading.

When Senior VP of Hardware Engineering John Ternus steps into the CEO role in September, the company could be facing a rough patch, but at least Apple isn’t alone in its supply struggles.

articles.title: Should you still buy your next smartphone — or subscribe to it instead? | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple's new Upgrade program is the latest sign that smartphone ownership is changing.
articles.body:
The smartphone industry’s next battleground may not be the phone itself, but how consumers get it. As premium devices become more expensive, Apple, Samsung, and others are betting that leasing, subscriptions, and guaranteed buyback programs can make upgrading more attractive.

This week, Apple launched Apple Upgrade in the U.S. in partnership with Klarna, allowing consumers to lease an iPhone, Mac, iPad, or Apple Watch for a monthly fee with the option to upgrade, return, or eventually purchase the device. Samsung, meanwhile, has been offering its Galaxy Forever program in India, combining financing with a guaranteed buyback to let consumers upgrade flagship Galaxy smartphones more predictably.

On Apple’s earnings call on Thursday, CEO Tim Cook said the Upgrade program is intended to make it easier for customers — particularly those who prefer upgrading on a regular schedule — to access the company’s latest products through a leasing plan. He also said Apple’s relatively high resale values make the model well suited to such plans.

The shift comes as consumers keep their smartphones for longer, driven by rising prices as tighter supplies push up memory and other component costs, and incremental hardware improvements that have kept older devices capable for longer. That has given manufacturers fewer opportunities to sell new devices while also reducing the flow of handsets into the booming refurbished market. Analyst firm Counterpoint Research expects the average global replacement cycle to stretch to four years in 2026, up from 3.5 years in 2025.

The trend is evident in the United States, where premium smartphone owners now keep their devices for an average of 42 months, up from 38 to 40 months in previous years, according to market intelligence firm IDC. That has prompted smartphone makers to experiment with leasing, subscriptions, and guaranteed buyback programs.

“These programs fundamentally do not work unless a secondary market exists,” said Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. “The only way to sustain a used or refurbished market is to make sure devices enter that market, and leasing and guaranteed buyback programs make that possible.”

The industry’s challenge, however, is not just to get consumers to upgrade more often — it is also to persuade them that these new ownership models make more financial sense than buying outright.

“Leasing definitely isn’t for everyone, but it can make sense, especially for someone who upgrades often,” Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at online lending marketplace LendingTree, told TechCrunch. Consumers who keep their phones for three, four, or five years, however, are often better off buying them outright than opting for a subscription or leasing model, he said.

For those who upgrade every year or two, however, the economics can be closer than they appear. “It’s important to stress the fact this is an upgrade program that’s done via a lease, rather than just a leasing program,” Weinbach said. “The intent is that the user will turn in their device every 12 to 36 months because they intend to upgrade regardless.”

Based on his analysis of Apple’s new program, Weinbach told TechCrunch that consumers who already replace their phones frequently could pay roughly the same — or, in some cases, even less — than they would by buying a device outright and trading it in later, particularly on higher-storage models whose trade-in values do not always reflect their higher purchase prices.

The programs, however, are not just about making premium smartphones more affordable. Smartphone makers also see them as a way to keep customers within their ecosystems as devices become more expensive and replacement cycles lengthen.

“The real driver isn’t shorter upgrade cycles; it’s protecting margin and retention as pricing pressure mounts,” IDC’s associate vice president of devices research Navkendar Singh told TechCrunch.

Rather than simply trying to get consumers to replace their phones more often, brands are increasingly trying to turn costly smartphone purchases into more predictable monthly payments that keep customers within their ecosystems, Singh said.

The idea of paying monthly for a smartphone is not new, particularly in the U.S., where wireless carriers have long offered financing and upgrade plans tied to service contracts. However, what is changing is that phone makers are increasingly trying to own that relationship themselves.

Carrier financing has long helped make premium smartphones more affordable in the U.S. “It’s the interest-free financing of 36 months and aggressive trade-ins of up to $1,100 that have made the U.S. the region with the highest smartphone average selling prices,” Nabila Popal, senior research director at IDC, told TechCrunch.

The existing financing and trade-in offers have helped Apple and Samsung dominate the U.S. smartphone market with a combined share of more than 80%, per IDC.

The shift toward subscriptions and other alternative ownership models is also creating opportunities for startups. BytePe , which offers subscription-style plans for smartphones and other consumer electronics in India, said more than 80% of its customers opt for subscriptions over outright purchases or traditional EMI plans.

Founder and CEO Jayant Jha told TechCrunch that BytePe’s typical customers are young professionals in their first or second jobs who want access to premium smartphones without paying the full price upfront or committing to long ownership cycles.

The trend is not limited to the U.S. and India. Companies such as the U.K.’s Raylo and Germany’s Grover have built businesses around leasing smartphones and other consumer electronics through monthly subscription plans.

Analysts expect more companies to follow. “The primary objective is to increase customer lifetime value by improving retention, creating predictable upgrade cycles, and securing a steady pipeline of trade-in devices for certified refurbishment and resale,” Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research, told TechCrunch.

Pathak expects such initiatives to become more common in the premium smartphone segment, although he believes financing will remain the more important tool for improving affordability.

Nonetheless, outright ownership is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. Mandeep Manocha, co-founder and CEO of Indian smartphone trade-in and refurbishment platform Cashify, expects leasing, subscriptions, and outright purchases to coexist rather than replace one another.

“All three business models have a place to exist, and they will continue to do so,” Manocha told TechCrunch. “There is a natural transition that may happen from complete ownership to leasing, but it’s a long journey.”

That may be especially true in the U.S., where carrier financing has long dominated premium smartphone purchases.

IDC’s Popal expects Apple’s new Upgrade program to have a bigger impact on Mac sales than iPhones, saying the offering is more likely to expand financing options than fundamentally change how Americans buy their next smartphone.

On Apple’s earnings call on Thursday, CEO Tim Cook said the Upgrade program is intended to make it easier for customers — particularly those who prefer upgrading on a regular schedule — to access the company’s latest products through a leasing plan. He also said Apple’s relatively high resale values make the model well suited to such plans.

The shift comes as consumers keep their smartphones for longer, driven by rising prices as tighter supplies push up memory and other component costs, and incremental hardware improvements that have kept older devices capable for longer. That has given manufacturers fewer opportunities to sell new devices while also reducing the flow of handsets into the booming refurbished market. Analyst firm Counterpoint Research expects the average global replacement cycle to stretch to four years in 2026, up from 3.5 years in 2025.

The trend is evident in the United States, where premium smartphone owners now keep their devices for an average of 42 months, up from 38 to 40 months in previous years, according to market intelligence firm IDC. That has prompted smartphone makers to experiment with leasing, subscriptions, and guaranteed buyback programs.

“These programs fundamentally do not work unless a secondary market exists,” said Max Weinbach, an analyst at Creative Strategies. “The only way to sustain a used or refurbished market is to make sure devices enter that market, and leasing and guaranteed buyback programs make that possible.”
The industry’s challenge, however, is not just to get consumers to upgrade more often — it is also to persuade them that these new ownership models make more financial sense than buying outright.

“Leasing definitely isn’t for everyone, but it can make sense, especially for someone who upgrades often,” Matt Schulz, chief consumer finance analyst at online lending marketplace LendingTree, told TechCrunch. Consumers who keep their phones for three, four, or five years, however, are often better off buying them outright than opting for a subscription or leasing model, he said.

For those who upgrade every year or two, however, the economics can be closer than they appear. “It’s important to stress the fact this is an upgrade program that’s done via a lease, rather than just a leasing program,” Weinbach said. “The intent is that the user will turn in their device every 12 to 36 months because they intend to upgrade regardless.”

Based on his analysis of Apple’s new program, Weinbach told TechCrunch that consumers who already replace their phones frequently could pay roughly the same — or, in some cases, even less — than they would by buying a device outright and trading it in later, particularly on higher-storage models whose trade-in values do not always reflect their higher purchase prices.

The programs, however, are not just about making premium smartphones more affordable. Smartphone makers also see them as a way to keep customers within their ecosystems as devices become more expensive and replacement cycles lengthen.
“The real driver isn’t shorter upgrade cycles; it’s protecting margin and retention as pricing pressure mounts,” IDC’s associate vice president of devices research Navkendar Singh told TechCrunch.

Rather than simply trying to get consumers to replace their phones more often, brands are increasingly trying to turn costly smartphone purchases into more predictable monthly payments that keep customers within their ecosystems, Singh said.

The idea of paying monthly for a smartphone is not new, particularly in the U.S., where wireless carriers have long offered financing and upgrade plans tied to service contracts. However, what is changing is that phone makers are increasingly trying to own that relationship themselves.

Carrier financing has long helped make premium smartphones more affordable in the U.S. “It’s the interest-free financing of 36 months and aggressive trade-ins of up to $1,100 that have made the U.S. the region with the highest smartphone average selling prices,” Nabila Popal, senior research director at IDC, told TechCrunch.
The existing financing and trade-in offers have helped Apple and Samsung dominate the U.S. smartphone market with a combined share of more than 80%, per IDC.

The shift toward subscriptions and other alternative ownership models is also creating opportunities for startups. BytePe , which offers subscription-style plans for smartphones and other consumer electronics in India, said more than 80% of its customers opt for subscriptions over outright purchases or traditional EMI plans.

Founder and CEO Jayant Jha told TechCrunch that BytePe’s typical customers are young professionals in their first or second jobs who want access to premium smartphones without paying the full price upfront or committing to long ownership cycles.

The trend is not limited to the U.S. and India. Companies such as the U.K.’s Raylo and Germany’s Grover have built businesses around leasing smartphones and other consumer electronics through monthly subscription plans.

Analysts expect more companies to follow. “The primary objective is to increase customer lifetime value by improving retention, creating predictable upgrade cycles, and securing a steady pipeline of trade-in devices for certified refurbishment and resale,” Tarun Pathak, research director at Counterpoint Research, told TechCrunch.
Pathak expects such initiatives to become more common in the premium smartphone segment, although he believes financing will remain the more important tool for improving affordability.

Nonetheless, outright ownership is unlikely to disappear anytime soon. Mandeep Manocha, co-founder and CEO of Indian smartphone trade-in and refurbishment platform Cashify, expects leasing, subscriptions, and outright purchases to coexist rather than replace one another.

“All three business models have a place to exist, and they will continue to do so,” Manocha told TechCrunch. “There is a natural transition that may happen from complete ownership to leasing, but it’s a long journey.”
That may be especially true in the U.S., where carrier financing has long dominated premium smartphone purchases.

IDC’s Popal expects Apple’s new Upgrade program to have a bigger impact on Mac sales than iPhones, saying the offering is more likely to expand financing options than fundamentally change how Americans buy their next smartphone.

articles.title: The global memory shortage hits the MacBook Air
articles.summary: The global memory chip shortage appears to be affecting the availability of Apple’s most popular Mac.
articles.body:
The global memory chip shortage is affecting the availability of Apple’s most popular Mac, according to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman .

Gurman said the shortage — caused by the demands of chip-hungry AI companies — had already affected Apple’s more niche computers, the Mac mini and Mac Studio. But it seems the company is now struggling to keep the MacBook Air in stock, with retailers saying that supply seems to be more constrained than ever before.

Indeed, anyone trying to buy a MacBook Air from the Apple website will have to wait until the back half of August — or for certain configurations, until September.

Gurman says Apple is working to address the issue by raising prices and sourcing memory from Chinese suppliers. Meanwhile, the company delayed its latest back-to-school promotion from June. And for the first time, the marketing material is more focused on the base model of the MacBook Pro. It even warns , “MacBook Air subject to availability.”

articles.title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
articles.summary: New CEO Toni Schneider discusses taking over for Jay Graber, the AT Protocol, his time at Automattic, how AI affects development, and communities like BlackSky.
articles.body: Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO. This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder, because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all. Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable. But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team. --- [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/chorus/uploads/chorus_asset/file/24792604/The_Verge_Decoder_Tileart.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- Toni was formerly the CEO of Automattic, which makes the huge WordPress web content management platform, and you’ll hear him make the case that this period in social networking feels a lot like the early days of the web, and that success looks like a vibrant ecosystem with lots of big players that might take a decade to fully develop. That’s quite a vision, but here and now, the open web is falling apart, and the social products of today are fragmenting and in many cases either get smaller or full of AI slop. So we talked about all of that, and about Bluesky’s reputation as a bastion of leftists insulated in their own little bubble sitting next to the increasingly hard right bubble of X. And of course, we talked about how Bluesky might start to generate revenue — and interestingly enough, it’s not just ads. This is a fun one that touches on almost every Decoder theme there is. I think you’re gonna like it. Okay: Bluesky CEO Toni Schneider. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Toni Schneider, you are a venture partner at True Ventures, and more importantly, the now permanent CEO of Bluesky. Welcome to Decoder. Thank you. Thanks for having me. I am very excited to talk to you. What is happening with the open social web is maybe the most important thing happening for media. It does not get as much attention as AI, but there’s something very big happening on these interoperable social networks. I know that you are a believer in it in the same way that you believed in the web when you were the CEO of Automattic, which is the company that makes WordPress. So let’s just start at the very start. Describe what you think Bluesky is today and what you think the opportunities with these new kinds of networks are. Bluesky today is really two things. There’s the Bluesky app, which is what a lot of people are familiar with. It’s a social network. We think it’s a better social network. It’s more human focused, doesn’t have ads. It doesn’t have algorithms. But more importantly, underneath Bluesky is an open protocol called AT Protocol. And Bluesky is only one of now over a thousand apps built on that protocol. The whole point of Bluesky was to demonstrate that this open protocol could scale and attract other builders, building lots of apps, lots of social experiences that all interoperate and connect with each other, which is what we believe the future of social media should look like. It’s what is actually going to make social media something that we believe in, which is that the future of social media should serve the public good. That is what motivates us, and that’s why we built the protocol first and then the app. There’s a lot in there already that is just pure Decoder bait, including the notion that Bluesky, the product, and the ATmosphere and AT Protocol, the standard, are all intermixed in one company that you now run. Right next to that is maybe the purest Decoder bait of all: the fact that Jay Graber, who was the CEO of Bluesky – she was on the show about two years ago – stepped down into the role of chief innovation officer. You were the interim CEO, and now after four months, you are the full-time CEO. Fundamentally, that is just the story that Decoder loves to tell the most. Talk me through that. What made you step in as the interim CEO, and why did you decide to become the full-time CEO? It’s actually really cool and inspiring that a founder, after she worked on this for six years, got it off the ground. She started inside Twitter, got it out of there, made it an independent thing. There are a lot of reasons why Bluesky is facing long odds and she got into this place, and then felt like it’s at a scale now where [it’s in] her sweet spot, the things that she loves working on, which is vision, innovation, new ideas. She felt pulled back towards building, especially also because of the advent of AI and how AI and AT Proto can interoperate. She felt like that’s what she wants to go work on, and it’s time to find somebody else for the CEO job. I was already involved with this project because I met the team a little bit over two years ago, probably around the same time Jay was on your podcast. We became investors through True Ventures. So I’ve been following it as an investor, supporting it. The team approached me and said that my background with WordPress and open source was a really good fit. And so I agreed to be interim CEO initially because I was still a general partner at True and it’s a firm I helped build. It’s an amazing firm that I didn’t want to leave behind. But also, at True, we’ve had this model where we’ve moved back and forth between operator and investor. I did that while I was running Automattic. So I stepped into it. After working on it hands-on for a few months, it just got more and more fun, more and more energizing. You just feel the momentum. Also, True just switched to a new fund. So actually the timing was good where I could say, “Okay, I will switch my true role to part-time, become a venture partner,” which is what I used to be when I ran Automattic, “and I’ll go all in at Bluesky.” Tell me about the difference between being the interim CEO and the full-time CEO. When you’re the interim CEO, it feels like there are probably some boundaries in what you can do. And then the full-time CEO can obviously do everything that a full-time CEO can do. What did you feel like the boundaries were as interim CEO? On the inside, it hasn’t felt very different. I actually think the move to drop the “interim” is more important on the outside, especially for the ATmosphere and the AT Proto community, and people building on this platform and in this ecosystem just to say, “No, I’m here for the duration. This isn’t just some interim gig and then somebody else is going to show up.” So I felt like, to the outside, that makes a big difference. On the inside, the job really hasn’t changed much.. So many of my conversations here in Decoder are really about the timescale of decisions. I’ll make the comparison to my newsroom because it’s easy and it’s easy to understand. Our reporters make decisions in like 30-minute increments. A story comes up, they write it, they publish it, they move on to the next thing. I make decisions maybe in like week- or month-long increments. What are we going to cover? Where are the resources going to go? It seems like in the interim CEO role, the timescale of those decisions is necessarily short or it has the appearance of being short. And then I’m reading your note that you published when you became the full-time CEO. In the very beginning of it, you say we’re at the very beginning of the story with a decade of exciting work ahead. And I’m wondering if the timescale of the decisions you’re making now are a decade. Yeah. It touches on something really fascinating with this project. In general with decision making, one of the frameworks I really like is the reversible and irreversible decisions. A lot of decisions we make are actually reversible. I like to optimize to just make those decisions quickly and then make sure you can undo the decisions if you need to change them. And then there are a few decisions that really do have very long-term implications. They’re much harder to reverse. With this project in particular, there are decisions made at this protocol level that we’re going to have to live with for a long time. There’s a part of the company in this community that thinks very, very, very long term. This is a protocol that is going to be around for decades already. It’s in enough use that it’s going to be around for a long time. Those decisions you really need to be careful about. Then it goes all the way to things we try in the product that work or don’t work. I wasn’t in the interim mindset as much because I am also an investor in the company, so I care very much about the long-term picture. What attracts me to this whole endeavor is that it can have a really important long-term impact. I always think about, okay, how will this play out? Does this truly serve the core mission? It’s okay to make some of these harder decisions now that won’t pay off for a long time because this is going to take a while. It’s not just one company. It’s already thousands of others that are building together. That’s just a different timeframe and decision-making process than your typical just “go fast, scale as quickly as possible” [methodology]. I like it. I’m comfortable with it. I just want to stick with Bluesky, the company that is both responsible for the standard and the protocol, and the product that a lot of end users love and sometimes hate. That is the core tension of the company. The user base of Bluesky is or is not interested in the development of AT Protocol, is or is not interested in the wider ATmosphere. Under Jay’s tenure, the company was very focused on building out the protocol because the product literally could not exist unless the protocol was robust enough to stand up the product. You could see that back and forth. I have always felt that the company is far more interested in the protocol than the product, that the product was merely there to show what people could do. But now the product is big. It might be waxing or waning. It will come to whether you need to turn it into TikTok or not. Tell me where you, as a CEO with a decade-long vision for all of this, see the balance inside of Bluesky between the product, the thing that looks like a Twitter app, and the protocol, the thing that should enable thousands upon thousands of other social experiences? I see the Bluesky app and the product as enabling the ATmosphere. It’s an on-ramp, or maybe a lobby to the ATmosphere where it’s just a great way to get lots of people in, get people exposed to the idea, and then realize as you use the product, “Oh, there are other things here. This isn’t just a microblogging app.” An example from the last couple of months that’s gone super well is this format called Standard Site that emerged. The history of that is that Bluesky’s a microblogging app. People are asking for longer-form posting. A bunch of other apps started popping up that were for newsletters and blogging. In particular, three apps called Leaflet, Pckt, and Offprint. They got together and said, “Hey, why don’t we define a format for all of us to work together on the ATmosphere for all of the posts that we publish?” We looked at it and said, “Great, we can now take that and surface it in our app.” So now, if you’re posting a blog post on Leaflet, it just shows up in the Bluesky app and we can make that a seamless experience. This went over really well to the point where now WordPress is supporting Standard Site and lots of other publishing platforms. They’re realizing the benefit of, “If I just publish to this new format now, it’s going to show up and work across all these other platforms without me having to do anything.” It’s caused this really nice ripple effect throughout the ecosystem where people can work together just by using this format. Nobody has to do deals with each other. Nobody has to get permissions and no money has to change hands. And it’s just taken off. I’m hoping more and more Bluesky users will see those kinds of integrations and go, “Oh, cool. I’m not just getting Bluesky content here. I’m getting content from all these other apps, all these other networks. And it just works. I don’t have to do anything. I don’t have to go sign up for 10 different apps. It’s just one signup, one account, and it just works.” You’re describing two different kinds of things. There’s a lot of work to be done at the protocol level. There’s a lot of work to be done to support new kinds of experiences like Standard Site. Then there’s Bluesky, a product which has 45 million people, and probably needs to be substantially bigger if it wants to be the aggregator for a massive network that can displace some of the other social products out there. That needs to be a lot of things to a lot of people. It needs to find different kinds of product market fit. How big is Bluesky the company now, and how is it structured to point in two different directions? We’re now at 50 people, still very small. The biggest challenge is clearly trying to do everything you’ve described with a small team. We do have an ecosystem of hundreds and thousands of others working on it, so that helps. We do our best to coordinate everyone. I would say we’re making good progress. We’re seeing good momentum, especially on the ATmosphere side. The things we look at are the number of daily active apps on the network, which has doubled since the beginning of the year. It’s about to hit a thousand. We look at SDK downloads for our tools that have tripled. It’s going to hit a million downloads a month by later this year. Those are the numbers that show that not only is it scaling, but we’re able to scale it with the team that we have. How is that team structured? About 50 people, all remote, structured into small teams. I’m a big believer that six to eight person teams, highly aligned, highly incentivized, and motivated are the way to get things done. Probably the only way to get things done. There are three core product teams. There’s the app team that deals with the Bluesky app. There’s the ATmosphere team that does all the developer-facing stuff. And then there’s a third product team called the exploration team, and that’s a new team that Jay has stood up and is running. We actually just launched a new version of the product they’re working on, Attie. Think of it as AI layered on top of the ATmosphere and what you can do with that. Those are our three core product teams, and they’re each customer-facing. Consumer-facing, developer-facing, and then we’ll find out from the AI product what the market fit is there. We have a bunch of support teams that support those three core teams and that are pretty typical. We’ve got a legal team, et cetera, et cetera. I would say it’s a team that’s a very low ego, high agency. That is kind of the ethos. Low drama, just a lot of get-shit-done energy. Really collaborative. Whenever I think about new social products and how they might scale, especially with explosive user growth – up until recently, the conventional wisdom is you’ve got to scale trust and safety and moderation linearly with the size of your user base. Maybe we’re going to add AI to this and that linear relationship will break, or maybe it’ll actually get even more costly because token spend will get more costly than having human moderators, or there’ll be more false positives and we’re going to be even angrier. So you have to have more humans in the loop. It’s really unclear to me how that’s going to work. You’ve obviously been scaling Bluesky as a consumer social product. Then you have the complexity of, “We’re hooking onto lots and lots of other products that are putting content in front of people.” How does the moderation layer work? And have you seen it be a linear increase in cost with the size of the network and the user base? Moderation is huge in any social product. In addition to our 50-person team, we do have contractors that help us with moderation. What we’ve done differently is that our whole moderation system is composable or pluggable. It’s not just us that can label content and moderate it. Anybody can do it and add labels. It’s part of the protocol. Anybody else who builds products can decide if they want to use those labels or not. So if somebody on our moderation team labels something as, let’s say, AI slop, everybody else who’s building in this ecosystem can take advantage of that piece of data. They don’t have to, but they can. So what we’re seeing and what we’ve seen is we have our moderation team, but then there are other teams that have decided to moderate label content the way they want. For example, maybe the first non-Bluesky project on the protocol was Blacksky. And it’s now become a thriving company on its own. It’s a team building all kinds of interesting things. And they started out by saying, “Hey, we want to build a version of this network that is optimized for Black users and their needs. And we want to have our own moderation policies.” And they are able to do that and plug that in. But everything they’re doing is still part of the larger network. And now there are hundreds and thousands of these kinds of systems. This has really helped where the moderation burden isn’t all on one team that has to scale and look at everything. There should be lots of different teams and lots of different systems because each network, each community has its own idea of what moderation should look like. So we feel like this kind of distributed moderation approach is more powerful. That said, yes, we’re continuing to scale up ours, but it’s manageable. It’s a lot of work, but it’s manageable. It’s worth it when the whole network can benefit from it. The next part of that story that’s going to be really interesting is that the biggest thing we’re actually working on with AT Proto, the next evolution of the protocol, is private data. We all know that the public square, public social networking has reached a certain scale. And there are a lot of people who want to retreat into more private spaces. We’ve seen explosive growth in group chats. We’re all in a million group chats. This has been the number-one request from our community, from our developers: “Let us build more private, membership-based, various versions of private spaces on this protocol.” We’re in the middle of building that. It’s a community effort. It’s rolling out very soon. Now, moderation moves and gets broken up into even more and smaller spaces. People can decide, “If I don’t like a network or I don’t like the way it’s moderated, [I can] go start my own.” Go start your own community. That’s the most interesting thing ahead of us, because right now everything on AT Proto is public. It can only be used for a completely public product. Once we enable private data, I think that it’s like 10 or 100X the number of use cases we can serve. Not to be reductive, but I think it’s useful to talk about this in comparison to other social products people might be more familiar with. With AT Protocol right now and the ATmosphere, everything is very public. The models in my head are Twitter, and RSS, and massive broad-based publishing platforms, right? One-to-many. I think what you’re describing is much more like a Reddit style approach, where you have smaller, closed communities. Some of them can be totally private unless you’re invited in. And yet, they’re still on the ATmosphere in some way. Is that right? That’s right. The trade-off has traditionally been that if you want to be on a launch network, you have to be on a public network. Or if you want to control, have ownership over your own community, you have to set up your own thing. You have to run your own server or you have to run your own forum. There’s clearly a need for that because there are lots of those out there. But the challenge is each one of those is now a little island. And you have to convince people. We think we can pull off as the best of both worlds. When you build a community or private space on AT Proto, it’s absolutely 100% owned by you. It’s not owned by Bluesky or by any company. It’s just like everything else on a protocol. It’s owned by the users, not by the platform. So it’s really truly yours. You can move it around. You can make all the decisions. But because it’s on a shared protocol, all of these communities plug together. You can go to a place like Bluesky and get all your notifications in one place. You can see what’s going on across everything. You just need one login, one place to check, but you still have the independence and the identity of these individual communities. That is something that no other platform can do right now. You’re either on the large platform owned and controlled place, or you run your own and you’re a little siloed. We think we can solve that. We see the energy behind this idea and the number of things people are already prototyping is very palpable. I have to ask you the other Decoder question because I’m very curious where this idea came from and how you decided to bet on it. How do you make decisions? What’s your framework for making decisions? I already talked a little bit earlier about the reversible and irreversible decisions. The hardest thing about running any project is that, especially if it’s successful, it’s just an endless flow of things you have to prioritize and decide on. I find you could make that a lot less daunting and exhausting if you move a lot of decisions into this category of “they’re not that big a deal.” Let’s make it easy to experiment and reverse things, and really only focus on the truly long-term impactful things that we have to get right. You have this lightness or almost playfulness about some of these things, where it’s just not that big a deal. Let’s just try something. Let’s be creative and improvisational about it. This is a lot of how Automattic runs. I actually credit a lot of that to Matt Mullenweg’s approach to first running an open-source project. Inside Automattic, there are a lot of jazz analogies because Matt started out as a jazz musician. Just this improvisational, “don’t take it so seriously if you don’t have to.” There are very serious decisions we have to make as well. For those, I like spending a lot of one-on-one time with the leaders, and then gathering and going through the list and talking through the trade-offs. Making sure that at least in a good cadence, monthly or maybe quarterly, we go through and make those hard trade-off decisions and don’t leave the room until we say, “No, we’re only doing these two things on the important list. We can’t do everything. Let’s voice all the ideas, but get to agreement on the few things we’re trying to get done. If we get those done, then we’re actually in good shape and we keep making forward progress.” That’s the ongoing flow that we go through, and it seems to be working. I have to call out an email I got from a listener, ex-Amazon, who said, “Everyone always comes on your show and talks about reversible decisions and irreversible decisions. And I just want to point out that if you have enough money and time, every decision is reversible.” And I said, “Yeah, that’s right. Especially at Amazon scale, that’s certainly right.” What’s the line for you? What makes the decision irreversible? How much money and how much time does it take to reverse it? To me, it’s less about the money. It’s more the time. Some things just take years to unwind. I think anything that has – let’s call it a five-year time horizon,  where it’d be really painful to change course. Or maybe on the positive framing, it’s more like, “If we get this right, we don’t have to think about it again for five years.” That’s the category of things where – people talk a lot about, for example, with startups, it’s your investors. Especially early on, the first investors you work with are going to be with you for five or 10 years. And that’s a pretty big decision. You shouldn’t just take the first check that comes along. You should really think that through because I’ve lived that. True has invested in 500 startups over the last 20 years, and we’ve seen every possible way that that plays out. That’s a good thing to really pay attention to early on, not just rush. Early in my career, I was like, “I just need money. Just give me a check and I’ll keep building. I just want to build things.” That’s an example of the timeframe where I feel like it’s really nice when it just works for several years. You [don’t] have to go back and invest more time, more money to reverse something. So I want to put two decisions in practice here. And your framing here is perfect for this question. You decided to be the CEO of Bluesky, to become the permanent CEO of Bluesky. You’re calling that a 10-year decision, right? It’s in your note. We’ve talked about it here. How did you make that decision? Did they come to you and say, “You’re going to be the CEO now. Sorry, we’re stripping the title away”? Did you have to write a memo? How did that all happen? It was a gradual process. The job is great. The team is great. The mission is what I want to work on for the next 10 years. So that was not a hard decision. It was really that I already had a job, and just figuring out a way to make those two pieces work together and to make a transition work. From early on, the Bluesky team and board said, “We think this is working really well. Can we make this permanent?” It was probably a couple months of just working through how a transition would work. So you were the interim CEO for two months, and you spent two months figuring out how the transition worked and then you became the permanent CEO? Yeah. Yeah, that sounds about right. It’s quite a timeline. The second one, maybe much more importantly is, “We’re going to make this big bet on private communities. We’re going to extend the protocol.” Logically, you’re going to have to extend the Bluesky app itself. You’re going to have to make a big bet on both the standard itself and how the consumer app will work. I would say, and maybe this is too reductive, the community on the Bluesky app does not like change, so you’re going to have to endure some change with them. “This is a bet. This is a big decision. This has to be the future of the protocol, the future of the ATmosphere.” How did you make that decision, and what made you convinced that it was the right one? The decision to extend the protocol has been underway. A year or two years ago, or maybe even from the very beginnings of the protocol, people said, “What are we going to do about private data?” So that’s been building, and it’s natural. Once people start building on your protocol, it’s the first question. “This is great, but I do have some private data.” Even inside the Bluesky app, we have DMs. Those aren’t on the protocol. We don’t want those out in the public. We have features inside the app that we had to build off protocol because it couldn’t support private data. So we have our own use cases. We got lots of them. That’s an obvious “we just have to do it.” How it affects the community, that’s what our app team is working through right now. One of the things that I feel like we’ve gotten better at in the last few months is to do that out in the open. Alex Benzer, who’s our head of product, who makes those decisions around what goes in the app and what doesn’t, has been posting about it and inviting feedback and saying, “Look, this is coming. What do you think? What kind of communities do you want? Do you want them? How similar should they be to the current app? How different?” I think we have 500 people who’ve signed up to give us feedback. We’re going through user interviews. People are already building communities on Bluesky actually because we have this functionality where people can make custom feeds. One of the huge differences in Bluesky is no algorithms. You get to make your own. You can plug in your own. People have made over 100,000 feeds. Some of those are really communities themselves. There are things like BookSky and AstroSky, where it’s just communities of people talking about a certain topic within a custom feed. People have taken what we have to bend it into a community shape. It’s already happening on a network. That makes it a lot less scary. It’s not like we’re going to stop one thing and pivot somewhere else. We’re just doing more of a thing that some users are already doing. I think we can do it in a way that doesn’t disrupt. If you never want to join a private community, you don’t have to. Bluesky the app as it stands today isn’t going to change. The public part of it is popular, it’s growing. So we’re not going to mess with that. Let me ask you about Bluesky the app not changing, because I think that’s the thing that I’m poking at. It feels like every other social network evolves into a crab. Everything is evolving into TikTok. We can see it happening every single day. Meta today announced a test in which the big blue Facebook app will open for some set of users into full-screen video. “Screw it. We’re just going to turn Facebook into TikTok.” Everything heads in that direction. X has headed in that direction. That’s the competition, and maybe that’s the thing the market wants. You’re saying, “We’re going to build private data. We’ll have a more Reddit-like experience.” Bluesky may be the last really text-first social platform of its kind that exists. Do you feel that pull into different directions, into different formats? Because that’s a thing that your user base also pushes against. This is the beauty of an open protocol. Let somebody else build the TikTok of AT Proto. Let somebody else go push into new formats. We’re perfectly happy with a text-first, microblogging network. We love it. Honestly, I’m glad if others are chasing off in other directions because we like what we have. We talked earlier about traffic. A lot of these other networks, as you know… You’ve coined the term Google Zero right there. All these walled gardens, all these other platforms are getting more and more walled. They say, “Once we’re open enough to attract an audience, and then once you’re here, we’re not going to let you go. We’re just going to keep trying to find ways to keep you in there.” Bluesky’s the opposite. Because of the protocol, it’s locked open by default. We couldn’t keep you in it even if we wanted to. We want people to build other apps and experiment with other things. We want people to find great content on Bluesky and leave. We’re still a place where we don’t downrank links. We love sending traffic to people. We send two million clicks a day to publishers. We’re the number-one referrer to a bunch of publishers, and we want to do more of that. We love the way that the open web works and people come to Bluesky to connect, to learn, to have fun, and then to find interesting things to go to. There’s no way we’re going to change that. I’m curious, if someone wants to build the TikTok of the ATmosphere, is there a bunch of protocol-level work that needs to be done to support it? I know there are attempts to do this. Skylight, I think, is a TikTok-like app on the ATmosphere. There are others. But all of your technical innovation on the standard itself is pointed at text. I’m wondering if there’s something you need to do to be better at video to compete with what all of the closed platforms are chasing at a much larger scale. No, I think at the protocol level, it’s easy to do. You can define your own records on the protocol. Yes, ours are text-focused or posts, they’re follows, they’re likes, things like that. But there are already people publishing all kinds of different things within a protocol. I saw yesterday that somebody’s publishing a patent database onto AT Proto, so everybody else can just tap into that patent information.
