articles.title: I finally found a magnetic phone grip I never want to remove
articles.summary: The $50 OhSnap Snap Grip Stand is excellent and does what most magnet rings don’t — stand your phone vertically.
articles.body: I told myself I wouldn’t buy an OhSnap accessory for my phone. Every one I’d tested was nice, but felt overpriced and slightly flawed. After I weighed in on the $40 Snap Grip 5 last year, I wound up sticking with my $25 Syncwire instead. But OhSnap’s $50 Snap Grip Stand finally got me. To have a truly useful vertical stand and grip always attached to my phone, ready at a moment’s notice? Heck yes. [Media: https://www.tiktok.com/@verge/video/7674258001020177677?lang=en] I started testing the Snap Grip Stand months ago, and soon discovered that I never took it off. So I bought my own. It’s thin — 3.7mm, so it slips effortlessly into my pocket without making an extra indent in my pants. It’s got a double-sided magnetic ring, like the previous gen, so it not only sticks to your magnet ring phone, it can stick flat against a fridge or gym equipment or my garage cabinets. It even lets some wireless charging through. Like the previous gen, the magnets hold my phone tightly, and the grip part is one of the most versatile I’ve tried. The clever interlocking joints can fit between two of your fingers loosely like a PopSocket, or you can put a finger through the joints for a very secure grip. The whole disc spins freely (though still with a bit of scraping noise) to rotate to any angle you like. But unlike the previous gen, the Stand has a stand unlike most other magnet grips on the market. The entire magnet ring is now encircled by a thinner fold-out ring on a hinged arm. Pull it down, and it effortlessly props up my phone in its normal vertical orientation. Most rival stands barely prop a phone, and even then they don’t deploy as fast. Here, there’s no need to take off the stand, or rotate it and lock a tab in place like OhSnap’s previous grips — pull out, plop phone on surface, done. [Image: OhSnap advertises that it’s “thinner than your camera bumps,” but that depends on whether you’re using a case. It’s thin enough. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-ohsnap-stand-sean-hollister-1-5.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] It’s not the only stand with such a design. The $17 Gornergrat Grat 5 has a similar stand and costs far less. But I tried one and found I don’t like its elastic strap, which feels loose and thus less secure around my fingers. OhSnap makes use of the extra vertical arm space to keep the stand from rotating when you don’t want it to: It’s got a extra vertical magnet in there to match Apple’s MagSafe pattern, as well as some grippy clear plastic material to provide friction. And I’m happy to say the aluminum gadget doesn’t seem to have any other unwanted coatings: I wasn’t a fan of the adhesive on the Snap Grip 4, or the soft-touch coating that started to peel when I tested the Snap Grip 5. Here, it appears to be bare anodized metal that looks and feels great. [Image: Neither of these phones (Pixel 9, Galaxy S25) has built-in magnets, but I bought magnet cases for each. Phone grips like this also come with adhesive magnet rings. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-ohsnap-stand-sean-hollister-1-6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Right now, I can only think of three things that’d make it better: a lower price, magnets in the stand’s ring (rather than the main ring) so I can use the magnets and the stand at the same time, and maybe a better way to open the grip one-handed. I do like how Tango’s spring-loaded grip can pop open when you press it. But I tried a Tango too, and I don’t like the way that spring feels between my fingers, pushing them apart too much. As for the lower price, at least OhSnap’s products are regularly on sale. I bought mine at Best Buy for $40 after tax.

articles.title: 8 things we learned from Google's Pixel 11 event
articles.summary: Google's Pixel 11 lineup introduces Magic Capture, HiLight notifications and proactive Gemini features designed to reduce screen time demands.
articles.body: Google packed a lot into its annual Made by Google event Aug. 12.  We got four Pixel 11 phones, a new Pixel Watch, Google's first finder tag and fresh Pixel Buds features. Yet one theme kept coming through. Google wants its devices to anticipate what you need before you have to ask. I was especially interested in what these upgrades could change in everyday use. A faster processor sounds nice. A phone that surfaces your flight information when someone texts you about a trip feels much more personal. FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING If you want to see how much has changed in one generation, take a look back at our coverage of the Pixel 10 event and Google's previous phones, smartwatch and earbuds.  Here are the eight things that stood out to me. New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers.  No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward. Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com. 1) Google's Pixel 11 lineup gets meaningful upgrades The phone lineup includes the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, Pixel 11 Pro XL and Pixel 11 Pro Fold. All four use Google's new Tensor G6 processor and are designed around its latest Gemini Intelligence features. The standard Pixel 11 gets a camera bar that is 40% thinner than earlier base-model Pixels. It also has a larger 48-megapixel main camera with 56% more light sensitivity than the Pixel 10. Its 5x telephoto camera now supports up to 30x Super Zoom.  The Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL have Google's brightest Pixel displays yet, reaching up to 3,600 nits. Google also says a new display coating provides more than twice the scratch resistance of the previous Pro generation. Its upgraded telephoto camera can reach up to 120 times Pro Zoom.  All three traditional Pixel 11 models now start with 256 GB of storage. Google also carries Pixelsnap magnetic wireless charging into the Pixel 11 lineup, with Qi2 support and faster wireless charging that can reach up to 25W on compatible models. Pixelsnap lets you snap on compatible chargers, stands, grips and other magnetic accessories. Then there is the Pixel 11 Pro Fold. Google made it almost 10% lighter and about 1 millimeter thinner than the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. A redesigned hinge, new back material and stronger outer display also make it three times more durable than last year's Fold, according to Google's testing. That gives the Pixel 11 family a clearer reason to upgrade beyond AI alone. Google has changed the cameras, durability and charging experience while refining the physical design. Google is also trying to make switching from an iPhone less painful. Quick Share on Pixel can now send and receive photos and videos with iPhones and MacBooks, while Google says your photos and group chats can move over when you switch. All four Pixel 11 phones are available for preorder now, including the Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro, Google Pixel 11 Pro XL and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. They officially go on sale Aug. 20. 2) Gemini gets much more proactive on Pixel 11 Google is taking another step toward making Gemini feel less like an app you open and more like something that can help across your phone. Gemini can now handle multistep tasks across more than 40 apps. Pixel 11 can also surface information based on what you are doing.  For example, if a friend messages you about an upcoming trip, a card can appear with your booking information and flight status. Pixel can also suggest actions based on your conversation. If you are discussing dinner plans, for example, it may offer a prompt to make a reservation. It can suggest adding an event to Calendar or saving a location to Maps. Google also introduced Rambler, a Gemini-powered voice input feature. It cleans up natural speech as it transcribes you. That means filler words such as "um" and "ah" do not have to end up in your finished message. That could be one of those small features you quickly start using every day. Much of this is powered by Google's new Tensor G6 processor. Google says Tensor G6 can process on-device AI tasks up to 3.5 times faster while using up to 3.5 times less energy than the previous generation under its testing. Google also introduced Sign To Text, which lets Pixel understand American Sign Language through the camera. Users can sign to write, chat or prompt Gemini from the keyboard. Google says the feature can recognize one-handed and two-handed signing along with facial expressions for grammar and tone. It is available for ASL now, with more sign languages planned. 3) Pixel 11 cameras want you to stop staring at the screen One of my favorite ideas from the event is Magic Capture. Instead of making you concentrate on hitting the shutter at exactly the right second, Magic Capture can analyze around 400 frames during a typical session. It then delivers carefully timed 12-megapixel photos. The feature can also automatically crop or unblur an image. At the same time, it saves video without making you switch camera modes. That could come in handy with kids, pets or anything else that refuses to pose for you. The hardware gets an upgrade too. Pixel 11 has a new 48-megapixel main sensor that Google says delivers 56% more light sensitivity than Pixel 10. Its 5x telephoto camera can reach 30x Super Zoom. Meanwhile, Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL get an upgraded 48-megapixel telephoto camera. Google says its larger sensor provides 30% more light sensitivity. The Pro phones can reach up to 120x Pro Zoom. Google says the new Instant Night Sight is four times faster, helping Pixel capture low-light photos without requiring you to hold the phone still as long.  There is also a new Camera Looks feature. It lets you choose a visual style before taking the photo. You can select a default look or customize additional styles to suit the shot. If the camera is your biggest reason for upgrading a phone, you may also want to compare the new Pixels with our current top Android phones of 2026 at cyberguy.com. 4) HiLight brings back the notification light with a twist Remember when phones had little notification lights? Google is bringing that idea back in a much more noticeable way. Pixel 11 Pro and Pixel 11 Pro XL introduce HiLight. Colored LED lights around the camera flash can glow while the phone is face down. For example, HiLight uses different patterns to show when Gemini is listening, thinking or responding. You can also assign colors to important contacts so an incoming call gives you a visual clue about who is calling. Google says message notifications from favorite contacts are among the capabilities planned for HiLight later. I like the thinking here. Phones are very good at pulling us back onto the screen. A quick visual signal could give you useful information without demanding your full attention. The Pixel 11 Pro Fold gets HiLight as well. 5) Pixel 11 puts more control around AI and security With Gemini getting access to more context on your phone, privacy was an obvious question at the event. Google says Pixel gives users visibility into what AI is doing and controls over how their data is used. You can also turn AI features on or off. Google highlighted several security protections built into Pixel 11. The phone can automatically block many spam calls and texts while warning you about messages or calls that may be scams. Google is also promising seven years of automatic security updates. An upgraded security chip is designed to help protect personal information stored on the phone. 6) Pixel Watch 5 moves deeper into health monitoring Pixel Watch 5 may be the device I would watch most closely after launch. Google upgraded its GPS and says route tracking can be twice as accurate as previous Pixel Watch generations in difficult environments. The watch also gets 50% more RAM and a faster processor compared with Pixel Watch 4.  Then there is Google Health. Pixel Watch 5 introduces Health Guardian features that look for longer-term changes in your wellness. These include monthly summaries involving blood pressure trends, sleep breathing quality and insulin resistance trends. Google says these features are designed for general wellness and are not intended to diagnose or treat medical conditions. The headline safety feature is Breathing Emergency Detection. It uses the watch's sensors and on-device AI to look for a severe, persistent drop in oxygen saturation. If the wearer becomes unresponsive, the watch can automatically call emergency services and transmit the person's location.  There is an important catch for U.S. buyers. Breathing Emergency Detection is available on Pixel Watch 4 and Pixel Watch 5 in select European countries. It is not available in the United States. Google says it plans to expand the feature to more countries. Pixel Watch 5 is available for preorder now and starts at $399 for the 41 mm model and $429 for the 45 mm version. The watches go on sale Aug. 20. 7) Pixel Tag finally gives Google its own item tracker Google is officially entering the finder-tag business. Pixel Tag is a small tracker for things such as keys, wallets or luggage. It connects to Google's Find Hub network, which includes more than 1 billion Android devices. That network can help locate an item when your own phone is no longer nearby.  When you are close to the tag, Ultra-Wideband with Bluetooth Channel Sounding can provide distance and directional guidance on compatible devices. You can also make the Pixel Tag play a sound. Interestingly, the button on the tag works in reverse too. Press it and you can ring your phone. Google says the replaceable battery lasts more than one year. The tag carries an IP67 water and dust resistance rating. You can also share a Pixel Tag with up to 10 people. Security matters with any location tracker. Google says Android phones automatically warn you if an unknown tag appears to be traveling with you. We have covered Google's expanding location tools before. You can read more about Find Hub and Google's Android security protections. Pixel Tag costs $29 for one or $99 for a four-pack. It is not available for preorder yet. Google says it goes on sale Nov. 11. Instead, it announced new software features and a new Olive finish. Google says an upgraded Active Noise Cancellation feature can compensate when the fit or seal changes, helping maintain noise cancellation while you are moving. Another clever feature connects the Buds with Pixel Watch. Later this year, your Buds will automatically pause audio if your Pixel Watch senses that you have fallen asleep. Google also says Live Translate improvements are coming to Pixel Buds Pro 2 and Pixel Buds 2a later this fall. Pixel Buds Pro 2 are also getting the new Olive color to complement this year's Pixel devices. The Pixel Buds Pro 2 are available now, with the new Olive color joining the lineup. Instead, some of the most interesting changes focus on reducing how much attention your devices demand. Magic Capture could make it easier to get the photo without experiencing the entire moment through your screen. HiLight could tell you whether a call matters before you pick up your phone. I am also watching the Pixel Watch 5 closely. A watch that can automatically call for help during certain breathing emergencies could become an important safety tool. articles.title: Amazon’s drones will soon deliver to nearly 500 US cities and towns
articles.summary: ﻿The Prime Air service has already delivered ‘hundreds of thousands of packages’ this year.
articles.body: Amazon says its drone delivery service will reach “nearly 500 cities and towns in the United States” by the end of this year, increasing its coverage by six times compared to the current footprint. Prime Air deliveries will soon be launched in the Chicago, Illinois; Syracuse, New York; Cleveland, Ohio; Atlanta, Georgia; and Boise, Idaho metro areas, according to Amazon’s announcement, with “more communities to come later this year.” These will join 11 locations across the US where Amazon already offers drone deliveries, with each Prime Air site serving an area of approximately 175 square miles. The service aims to quickly deliver packages of up to 5 pounds or less, and according to Amazon Prime Air vice president David Carbon, has already been used to deliver “hundreds of thousands of packages to customers” this year, with most orders arriving around 60 minutes after checkout. Amazon reiterated its drone safety features alongside these expansion plans, including Prime Air’s “industry-leading Detect-and-Avoid system.” That’s likely an attempt to minimize any concerns raised by the communities where the service is expanding, given these drones have already been scrutinized for crashing into cranes, internet cables, gardens, and an apartment building.

articles.title: DJI Osmo fans are breaking the shackles of its closed-source camera app
articles.summary: Osmosis, a free open-source app built by DJI watcher Konrad Iturbe, lets you wirelessly review, trim, and download DJI Osmo footage.
articles.body: Even if you love DJI’s drones and cameras, you might not love the company’s bloated closed-source apps that phone home to its cloud servers. But they’re the only way to easily review, manage, and wirelessly download your pocket camera’s footage on the go. Osmosis, a free open-source app built by DJI watcher Konrad Iturbe (with help from Claude) is an attempt to change that. By reverse engineering the protocol DJI’s cameras use to talk to the official Osmo app, he built his own — which not only lets you download files, but also see thumbnails, stream low-res previews, trim clips down to size, set favorites, filter out only photos or videos or favs, and queue up just the downloads you want. [Image: Here’s the media grid; you can tap any of those four teal buttons to filter or multi-select. You can see my SD card is mostly full, and I have 85 percent battery remaining. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-osmo-pocket-4p-sean-hollister-1-8.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] I just got it working on my Osmo Pocket 3 and the Osmo Pocket 4P that I easily bought in the US; it’s also been tested on the Osmo Nano, Osmo Action 5 Pro, Osmo Action 6, and it should work on the Xtra versions of those cameras too. [Image: This is a live low-res preview streaming from the camera to the phone. Intriguingly, I can optionally preview, and/or download files, while recording on the camera itself. The pencil button takes me to the edit-and-trim mode. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-osmo-pocket-4p-sean-hollister-1-9.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] The app isn’t all that polished yet. While it’s pretty easy to pair a new camera — it automatically detects your camera wirelessly and the app can remember more than one — it always takes longer than I’d like to connect and begin paging through my media. [Image: Press a pairing button on the app, then this screen automatically pops up on my camera. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-osmo-pocket-4p-sean-hollister-1-6.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Osmosis also doesn’t fully stow the gimbal on my Osmo Pocket 3 the way it does on the 4P below, so the lens is left exposed unless I manually fold it away. And when you’re filtering by Faved, you’re filtering the ones that you’ve hearted in Osmosis, not the ones you’ve hearted on the camera itself. [Image: Here it is connected to the Osmo Pocket 4 Pro, where it does stow the gimbal automatically. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/verge-osmo-pocket-4p-sean-hollister-1-10.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] But it might already be good enough for my Today I’m Toying With videos. I’m always left wondering if I “got the shot” on the Osmo Pocket 3’s tiny screen, I never want to fire up the DJI Mimo app to check, and so I always wind up overshooting and transferring lots of footage I don’t need. Now, perhaps I’ll just review it all, delete what I don’t want, trim what I do, and make my selects in Osmosis instead. Osmosis isn’t the only open-source app coming to replace DJI’s Mimo. I’m looking forward to trying OpenPocketCine, an ambitious field monitor app for the Osmo Pocket lineup that offers custom LUTs (which I as an amateur don’t use) and things like focus peaking and zebras (which I absolutely would because it’s tough to gauge focus and exposure on the Pocket’s tiny screen). It’s from the developer of OpenZCine for Nikon Z cameras, which I also haven’t tried yet.

articles.title: Oura faces lawsuit accusing it of misleading consumers about sleep-tracking accuracy | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The lawsuit alleges that Oura rings are unable to measure any of the physiological signals needed to assess sleep quality or determine sleep stages.
articles.body:
A proposed class action lawsuit is accusing smart ring maker Oura of deceiving consumers about the accuracy of its sleep tracking features.

The lawsuit, filed on Thursday by Clarkson Law Firm in San Francisco, alleges that Oura rings are unable to measure any of the physiological signals needed to assess sleep quality or determine sleep stages, and that they instead rely on AI-generated estimates that have “a coin flip’s chance of being correct,” according to the complaint .

The lawsuit follows years of Oura users taking to the internet to share their frustration with the smart ring’s sleep accuracy, with some saying they felt they slept poorly but were told their sleep had been optimal. Some have also expressed doubts about the device’s ability to monitor and detect sleep cycles.

“To capitalize on consumers’ desire for a tracker that could actually track sleep and monitor their sleep cycles, Oura sold expensive tracking rings, priced at $300 and up, advertising exactly that: that Oura rings are capable of seeing what only a hospital sleep lab can see, including the four different stages of sleep,” the complaint reads. “Oura did not just claim to measure a heartbeat or a temperature, but the exact stage of sleep the wearer is in—which in reality requires electrodes in the scalp and sensors on the eyes, as only a hospital or other clinical setting can do.”

Despite this, the complaint alleges that Oura marketed its ring as being “built for accuracy” and offering “unparalleled accuracy.” It says Oura told customers its smart rings could achieve 79% accuracy in their measurements, and more recently claimed that the rings offered 95% sleep-staging accuracy compared with clinical sleep labs.

The complaint goes on to allege that Oura cannot measure sleep or cycles because “sleep happens in the brain, not on one’s finger.”

“When people rely on a device to guide decisions about their health, misinformation cannot be tolerated,” said Ryan Clarkson, co-founder and managing partner at Clarkson Law Firm, in an emailed press release. “Oura users trust that the numbers on their screen reflect reality. People structure their days, interpret the way they feel, and design their lives around inaccurate figures spit out by these devices. Marketing an inaccurate sleep tracker as precise and reliable is dangerous because people believe it – and change their behavior accordingly.”

The complaint calls on Oura to stop deceiving consumers by falsely advertising its wearables as having capabilities they don’t deliver. It also seeks injunctive relief to prevent Oura from continuing to misrepresent its products, as well as restitution for consumers who purchased the products based on those allegedly false claims.

After this story was published originally, a spokesperson for Oura sent the following statement: “We stand behind our science, research, and accuracy claims. Like other consumer sleep wearables, Oura Ring estimates sleep stages using multiple physiological signals, including heart rate, heart rate variability, movement, breathing patterns, and temperature. There is well-documented, peer-reviewed independent scientific evidence that sleep stages are associated with distinct, measurable, reproducible changes in physiology, which is why these signals are reliably used to classify sleep stages.

“While Oura Ring is not a medical device or a substitute for a clinical sleep study,” said the company, “Oura’s sleep staging has been validated and compared favorably in multiple studies against polysomnography, the gold standard . . .Multiple third-party, independent studies support our claims of accuracy and we have transparently reported on the mechanisms and measures that inform Oura’s sleep staging.”

The statement continued on to say that Oura disputes the allegations and “will defend against them in the appropriate legal forum.”

articles.title: An okay laptop with 16GB of RAM is better than a nice laptop with 8GB, and this $520 HP OmniBook proves it
articles.summary: HP’s 16-inch OmniBook 3 wouldn’t normally be anything to write home about, but this affordable laptop with 16GB of RAM hits different in a world rocked by RAMageddon.
articles.body: Laptop prices are out of whack. $500 used to get you a tolerable laptop, and $900 got you a really good one. They often had similar CPU, RAM, and storage options because that stuff was comparatively cheap; the difference was often in build quality and screen rather than power. But RAMageddon has thrown everything off. Even laptops like the $950 Surface Laptop now start with 8GB of RAM, which isn’t enough. And on the lower end, where manufacturers are struggling to compete with the $700 MacBook Neo, they’re cutting corners on storage, CPU, and build quality too. However, one low-cost laptop has bucked this and genuinely surprised me. HP’s 16-inch OmniBook 3 is a basic productivity laptop that regularly goes for around $520 at Walmart and Amazon. It has Qualcomm’s base Snapdragon X chip, meaning passable everyday performance and excellent battery life. But it also has a humdrum screen, mediocre speakers, a run-of-the-mill trackpad, and a plastic build. Pre-RAMageddon, it would be nothing to write home about.  But 16GB of RAM and a 512GB SSD in an okay laptop for around $500? That counts as good news in 2026. [Product: 2026 HP OmniBook 3 16 (Snapdragon X) | https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0GVQTR19V?tag=theverge02-20, https://goto.walmart.com/c/482924/565706/9383?u=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.walmart.com%2Fip%2FHP-OB3-16-SnapdragonX-16-512-Silver%2F18515423351] The entry-level OmniBook 3 I tested has an 8-core Snapdragon X processor, 16GB of RAM, 512GB SSD, and a 16-inch 1920 x 1200 anti-glare IPS LCD. And the OmniBook 3 is fairly portable for a larger laptop with lots of ports. It’s barely heavier than a 14-inch MacBook Pro, and at a maximum thickness of 0.63 inches / 16mm it’s decently thin. This big laptop doesn’t feel big. And despite a plastic chassis and low price it doesn’t feel too cheap either. --- Component report card * Screen: D * Webcam: C * Keyboard: C * Trackpad: C * Port selection: B * Speakers: D * Number of ugly stickers to remove: 2 --- As much as I would like to see more cheap Windows laptops with the sleek looks and sturdy all-metal build of the MacBook Neo, I wouldn’t mind if more of them were like the OmniBook 3. Its screen, keyboard, trackpad, and webcam are all at least passable to decent. There isn’t anything special here, but unlike the Chuwi UniBook there’s also nothing that feels like a punishment.  The 1920 x 1200 / 60Hz screen isn’t high-quality or bright enough to combat the sun when taken outside (it maxes out at 300 nits of brightness and covers a paltry 62.5 percent of the sRGB color space), but it isn’t washed out or bleeding light at its edges. The mechanical trackpad has a basic diving board-style hinge, but a confident and decent-feeling kachunk-y click. The 1080p webcam is actually fairly sharp, and it does a good job handling backlight from a bright window — with only a hint of green color cast. But hey, at least it has Windows Hello face unlocking. And at least this not-too-large large laptop has lots of ports and charges via USB-C with a very compact 65W GaN charger. [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0007.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0014.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] My biggest gripe is the dual speakers (unsurprisingly), which lack bass and sound too treble-y, but they’re just tolerable enough to live with. My next biggest is the keyboard (surprisingly). I usually like HP keyboards, but this one feels too stiff. If you’re the type to hammer your fingers down and you love a generously sized number pad you might be fine, but I get more typos than I’m used to from keys not registering. I could learn to live with it, but I’d still prefer not to have to. What I can totally live with is the performance. The OmniBook’s 8-core Snapdragon X processor is a little slower than the one in the $950 Surface Laptop I tested, but the OmniBook’s day-to-day performance is better because it’s not starved for RAM and its larger SSD is a little faster. Like other lower-end Snapdragon laptop chips it’s not going to wow you with graphics performance or tackle heavy content creation in Adobe apps, but it’s perfectly adequate for everyday multitasking work. Even when running several apps with a couple dozen Chrome tabs left open, including a video podcast playing, I didn’t feel it slow down the way the Surface Laptop or Chuwi UniBook, each with only 8GB of RAM, did.  And while a Snapdragon chip means this Windows laptop isn’t ideal for gaming, it does make it great on battery. You can pretty easily get around 12 hours of mixed web usage with a bit of music or video streaming. It feels like the money went into the core specs of the OmniBook 3, and HP just barely stuck the landing on the right compromises elsewhere. As much as I adore the build quality of Microsoft’s Surface Laptops, if I were spending my own money I’d choose the OmniBook 3, never worry about how much RAM is in use, and save over $400.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0013.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0005.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0017.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] If we reviewed the OmniBook 3 a year ago I might feel different, but it’s been a tiny breath of fresh air to use something this cheap and mostly think, “Not too bad!” Especially coming right after I tested the $450 Chuwi UniBook. An employee being issued this laptop for work shouldn’t feel like their IT department totally hates them. And while I think a MacBook Neo would still be a better all-around experience for a school-age kid, I’d totally understand saving nearly $200 to get the OmniBook 3 if a budget can’t be stretched.  My only worry is that the OmniBook 3’s price will go up like everything else. While there are more sub-$800 laptops coming, and I’ll be testing more very soon, the OmniBook 3’s price — and that of the OmniBook 5 I reviewed back in December — feel anomalous right now. The RAMageddon storm could eventually ruin them like it did many other laptops and devices. But, for now, there’s some safe harbor with this lowly OmniBook. --- HP OmniBook 3 16 specs (as reviewed) * Display: 16-inch 1920 x 1200 60Hz IPS LCD, 300 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100 (8 cores) * GPU: Adreno X1-45 * RAM: 16GB LPDDR5x * Storage: 512GB NVMe M.2 SSD * Webcam: 1080p IR camera * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3 * Ports: 2x USB-C (10Gbps, DisplayPort 1.4, Power Delivery 3.0), 2x USB-A (5Gbps), HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm audio jack * Biometrics: Windows Hello face unlock * Weight: 3.65 pounds / 1.66kg * Dimensions: 14.12 x 9.91 x 0.58 to 0.63 inches / 358.65 x 251.71 x 14.73 to 16mm * Battery: 68Wh (65W USB-C charger included) * Price: about $520 --- Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

[Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0007.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0006.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0014.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] My biggest gripe is the dual speakers (unsurprisingly), which lack bass and sound too treble-y, but they’re just tolerable enough to live with. My next biggest is the keyboard (surprisingly). I usually like HP keyboards, but this one feels too stiff. If you’re the type to hammer your fingers down and you love a generously sized number pad you might be fine, but I get more typos than I’m used to from keys not registering. I could learn to live with it, but I’d still prefer not to have to. What I can totally live with is the performance. The OmniBook’s 8-core Snapdragon X processor is a little slower than the one in the $950 Surface Laptop I tested, but the OmniBook’s day-to-day performance is better because it’s not starved for RAM and its larger SSD is a little faster. Like other lower-end Snapdragon laptop chips it’s not going to wow you with graphics performance or tackle heavy content creation in Adobe apps, but it’s perfectly adequate for everyday multitasking work. Even when running several apps with a couple dozen Chrome tabs left open, including a video podcast playing, I didn’t feel it slow down the way the Surface Laptop or Chuwi UniBook, each with only 8GB of RAM, did.  And while a Snapdragon chip means this Windows laptop isn’t ideal for gaming, it does make it great on battery. You can pretty easily get around 12 hours of mixed web usage with a bit of music or video streaming. It feels like the money went into the core specs of the OmniBook 3, and HP just barely stuck the landing on the right compromises elsewhere. As much as I adore the build quality of Microsoft’s Surface Laptops, if I were spending my own money I’d choose the OmniBook 3, never worry about how much RAM is in use, and save over $400.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0013.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0011.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0002.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0001.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0005.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0003.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/268709_HP_OmniBook_3_16_laptop_review_ADiBenedetto_0017.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] If we reviewed the OmniBook 3 a year ago I might feel different, but it’s been a tiny breath of fresh air to use something this cheap and mostly think, “Not too bad!” Especially coming right after I tested the $450 Chuwi UniBook. An employee being issued this laptop for work shouldn’t feel like their IT department totally hates them. And while I think a MacBook Neo would still be a better all-around experience for a school-age kid, I’d totally understand saving nearly $200 to get the OmniBook 3 if a budget can’t be stretched.  My only worry is that the OmniBook 3’s price will go up like everything else. While there are more sub-$800 laptops coming, and I’ll be testing more very soon, the OmniBook 3’s price — and that of the OmniBook 5 I reviewed back in December — feel anomalous right now. The RAMageddon storm could eventually ruin them like it did many other laptops and devices. But, for now, there’s some safe harbor with this lowly OmniBook. --- HP OmniBook 3 16 specs (as reviewed) * Display: 16-inch 1920 x 1200 60Hz IPS LCD, 300 nits, anti-glare * CPU: Qualcomm Snapdragon X X1-26-100 (8 cores) * GPU: Adreno X1-45 * RAM: 16GB LPDDR5x * Storage: 512GB NVMe M.2 SSD * Webcam: 1080p IR camera * Connectivity: Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.3 * Ports: 2x USB-C (10Gbps, DisplayPort 1.4, Power Delivery 3.0), 2x USB-A (5Gbps), HDMI 2.1, 3.5mm audio jack * Biometrics: Windows Hello face unlock * Weight: 3.65 pounds / 1.66kg * Dimensions: 14.12 x 9.91 x 0.58 to 0.63 inches / 358.65 x 251.71 x 14.73 to 16mm * Battery: 68Wh (65W USB-C charger included) * Price: about $520 --- Photography by Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

articles.title: Amazon just hiked the prices for Echo, Fire TV, and Kindle products by up to 60 percent
articles.summary: Amazon’s hardware just got more expensive, as increases tied to RAM and storage costs are drivingup prices for Kindle, Echo, and Fire TV devices.
articles.body: Citing “significant increases in memory and storage component costs,” Amazon has raised prices on Echos, Kindles, Fire TVs, and Eeros by up to 60 percent, as first reported by Fortune. The cheapest products in Amazon’s lineup were hit hardest, with the Echo Dot smart speaker jumping from $49.99 to $79.99. The Fire TV Stick 4K Max also rose by over 40 percent to $84.99, and the base level Kindle now costs $149.99, a nearly 37 percent increase. In a statement to The Verge, Kristy Schmidt, senior communications manager of Amazon’s Devices & Services division, said, “The consumer electronics industry is facing significant increases in memory and storage component costs. After absorbing these increases for as long as we could, we recently adjusted pricing across our product lines. Our approach has always been to offer great products at accessible prices, and that commitment hasn’t changed.” Amazon’s flagship Echo Dot Max smart speaker, which launched last year, now costs $119.99, up from $99.99. Apple increased the price of its comparable HomePod Mini this summer to $129 from $99.99, also in response to rising costs. The Google Home Speaker remains at $99.99 for now. Amazon hardware products apparently not affected include its line of Ring cameras and video doorbells, and the Echo Studio, its higher-end $219.99 smart speaker. Here’s a full list of the price increases: Updated August 22nd: Added a statement from Amazon.

articles.title: Linkdaze’s smart calendar is built to run a household, not just track a schedule | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Linkdaze's smart digital calendar stands out for not putting its features behind a paywall, including an AI meal planner tool.
articles.body:
With back-to-school season approaching (or already here in some places), keeping track of everyone’s schedules can get pretty chaotic. Between work, school, appointments, sports, chores, and everything else going on, a regular paper calendar just doesn’t cut it. That’s where Linkdaze’s smart digital calendar comes in — a touchscreen tablet built specifically to organize a household rather than a single person.

One of Linkdaze’s biggest strengths is its calendar compatibility. The system can synchronize calendars from popular services, including Google, iCloud, Outlook, Yahoo, and Cozi, which is a dedicated family-organizing app. This is particularly useful for families where different members use different platforms. Instead of asking everyone to switch to a single calendar app, Linkdaze brings multiple schedules together and uses color coding to make individual family members easy to identify.

Launched last December, Linkdaze is available in 15.6-inch and 10.1-inch models, giving you some flexibility depending on how much wall space you have. Beyond calendars and appointments, you can use it for chores and rewards, meal planning, shopping lists, and other family organization. It can even double as a digital photo frame for displaying family photos.

The most interesting feature, however, is Linkdaze’s AI meal planner with “Snap-to-Sync.” Instead of manually entering everything into a meal-planning app, you can take a photo of a paper recipe or your kid’s school lunch menu. Linkdaze will turn that information into a digital meal plan and generate a shopping list from it. While not an entirely new idea, it’s a useful feature that helps Linkdaze stand out from a basic digital calendar.

Another big plus is that Linkdaze doesn’t require a monthly subscription for its main features. It’s an interesting choice in a category where recurring revenue has become the default. Skylight, a competing smart-calendar brand, offers additional features through its $79 per year subscription. For a hardware company entering a crowded smart-display market, that decision is either going to differentiate its product or look like a lost revenue stream.

Linkdaze is also less expensive up front, with the 10.1-inch model priced at $119.99 (currently discounted to $66 on Amazon ) compared with Skylight’s 10-inch model starting at $149.99 (if you pay for the subscription.)

Overall, this device could make a practical gift for busy parents who are trying to keep everyone’s schedules in one place. It could also be a great fit for college apartments, where roommates can use it to coordinate chores, study schedules, shared meals, and other household responsibilities. It’s also very helpful for those of us juggling interviews, deadlines, meetings, and story assignments.

This post was first published on August 20, 2026.

articles.title: New TV shows to watch this week: Tune in to ‘Lanterns’ on HBO, stream ‘My Brilliant Career’ on Netflix and revisit ‘Heroes’ on Tubi
articles.summary: Kyle Chandler and Aaron Pierre sink their teeth into a superhero adaptation, while Netflix releases a delightful Australian period romance.
articles.body:
Hey TV watchers! TV critic Michel Ghanem here. Every two weeks, I highlight the shows worth your TV time for Trust Me, I Watch Everything . Whether you prefer sticking to cable, catching the latest on streaming or digging up a hidden gem that slipped through the cracks, I try to curate something for everyone.

Can you believe summer is coming to a close? A few late August series have arrived to keep us entertained before the fall TV season is upon us. This week, consider tuning in to Adults, a low-stakes hangout comedy airing on FXX, or the HBO superhero adaptation Lanterns . Over on streaming, Netflix's My Brilliant Career is for those who love a period drama with a love triangle. Finally, in light of Hayden Panettiere's tragic death at 36, consider revisiting her breakout role in Heroes on Netflix or Tubi. Plus, a few other recommendations below.

Why you should watch it: Debatably, the Green Lanterns of the DC Comics aren't the flashiest superheroes. They are not mutants with superhuman abilities. Rather, the Lanterns are ordinary humans and aliens alike who wield superpowered rings provided by an intergalactic enforcement agency that help them fly, create force fields and project various green objects. Basically, they're the universe's police force — with rings they need to charge periodically, lest they find themselves completely ordinary without them.

Luckily, Lanterns is in good hands. The eight-episode drama is created by Chris Mundy ( Ozark ), Damon Lindelof ( Watchmen ) and comic book writer Tom King. Kyle Chandler stars as Hal Jordan, a former pilot and member of the Green Lantern Corps responsible for keeping Earth safe from extraterrestrial threats. He's also been training his recruit, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), for many years.

The two men get caught up in an incident in the small town of Rushville, Neb., where Hal quickly butts heads with local sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald) over how to handle a suspicious shooting. It all spirals into something much bigger, with a cast that also features Garret Dillahunt, Poorna Jagannathan, Jason Ritter and Nathan Fillion (reprising his hilariously grating Justice Gang member Guy Gardner from Superman ).

I wouldn't watch expecting the show to immediately jump into bright-green action sequences like an animated Justice League episode ; there's definitely more intrigue and story-building in these early episodes as we find out more about what's actually happening. Lindelof's Watchmen came out swinging from the jump, but this show has more of a True Detective slow burn.

In the spectrum of superhero adaptations on television, Lanterns is a very decent and engaging offering. It's accessible enough that you don't need to have watched anything else in the DC extended universe to jump in, and there's enough sci-fi suspense to keep you anticipating the next episode.

How to watch: New episodes of Lanterns stream every Sunday at 9 p.m. ET on HBO Max and air simultaneously on HBO.

Why you should watch it: Will there ever be another Friends ? Sitcoms about tight-knit friend groups who may or may not date each other are in rare supply these days. Adults , created by The Tonight Show comedy writing duo Ben Kronengold and Rebecca Shaw, might just be filling that gap.

We follow a group of post-college 20-somethings who all live together in their friend Samir's (Malik Elassal) house. The group in question includes Billie (Lucy Freyer), a stress-prone journalism major working in media; Anton (Owen Thiele), a remote worker with the special ability to befriend pretty much anyone; and Issa (Amita Rao), who is working overtime to get the household to accept her Canadian boyfriend, Paul Baker (Jack Innanen), into their crew.

It's all funny misadventures and dinner parties gone wrong, but half the fun is the scenes packed with bits and witty dialogue. I can't yet divulge anything juicy from the second season, which premieres on Aug. 27, but I can confirm there are some exciting guest stars (like Zosia Mamet, Raven-Symoné, Gaten Matarazzo) and a very queer love triangle set up in the first season's finale. Take this as your sign to catch up before it returns.

Adults is an easy recommendation in a television landscape with bloated episodes and an over-reliance on murder mysteries. The stakes are low in comparison, and episodes clock in at around 25 minutes, are tightly structured and move quickly. Before you know it, you'll feel right at home with your new group of friends.

How to watch: The new season of Adults premieres on Thursday, Aug. 27 at 9 p.m. ET on FXX with two episodes. Episodes will stream simultaneously on Hulu .

Why you should watch it: If you loved The Other Bennet Sister , Little Women and/or Bridgerton , you should make your way expeditiously to watch Netflix's new Australian period drama, My Brilliant Career , created by Liz Doran.

Based on the 1901 novel of the same name by Miles Franklin (and previously adapted as a film in 1979), the series stars Philippa Northeast as Sybylla Melvyn, a sassy aspiring writer stuck in the rural town of Possum Gully. She's encouraged by her family to move to Caddagat with the hopes of both furthering her writing career and finding a husband along the way. (Sybylla has little to no interest in centering a search for a partner, but since her family's financial future depends on it, the pressure is on.)

Life in Caddagat with her wealthy grandmother, Winifred (Anna Chancellor), and her widowed aunt, Helen (Genevieve O'Reilly), is a little different. There are rules of early 1900s society in place here; decorum and expectations of dress must be considered. But Sybylla has little regard for these aspects of higher society. She just wants to write her modern poetry in peace — and snort while she laughs without someone pointing it out.

Things take a turn when she meets two potential suitors: Harry Beecham (Christopher Chung), a very muscular Chinese Australian, and Frank Hawden (Jake Dunn), an English foreman. This is when the story leans more toward a typical love triangle affair as Sybylla finds herself unexpectedly yearning for romance, but it's all enjoyable enough to watch.

The series moves quickly across six episodes and is energetic, using an anachronistic soundtrack and some nice-looking cinematography that elevate it beyond the usual Netflix fare. Sybylla is easy to root for, even at her most chaotic. My Brilliant Career is a very strong entry in the romance-period-drama genre for those willing to take the plunge.

How to watch: All six episodes of My Brilliant Career are streaming on Netflix.

Outer Banks: The compelling teen drama set in North Carolina first premiered in 2020, and now returns for its fifth and final season . It remains one of Netflix's most popular series, and some of the cast — Drew Starkey in particular — have broken out to broader career success. See what's in store for one final adventure with the Pogues. — Now streaming on Netflix .

Why you should watch it: In light of Hayden Panettiere's untimely death , you may want to revisit her breakout role as Claire Bennet in NBC's iconic superhero drama, Heroes .

The landscape of superhero television has changed drastically since 2006. Marvel hadn't yet found the foothold it now has, and it was bold to debut an original series that bore a vague resemblance to X-Men without the foundation of comic books or previous films. Having recently rewatched the first season, I can confirm the series still holds up and should be held up as an example of how to make a propulsive, character-driven series that balances an overall plot with smaller, disparate arcs.

The show had a large ensemble cast, with high schooler Claire (Panettiere) playing a pivotal role when a prophecy sets Peter Petrelli (Milo Ventimiglia) on a mission to "save the cheerleader, save the world." The other heroes in question include Hiro Nakamura (Masi Oka), who has the ability to teleport and manipulate time; Nathan Petrelli (Adrian Pasdar), Peter's brother, who can fly; Matt Parkman (Greg Grunberg), a police officer and mind-reader; and Niki Sanders (Ali Larter), who finds out she has a split personality with a much stronger, brazen version of herself.

Each character gets a piece of the story as they discover their abilities, but become connected when the story's villain, Sylar (Zachary Quinto), begins eliminating the superpowered one by one in the most horrific way possible — sawing open their heads and consuming their brains, absorbing their abilities in the process.

There's also an organization hunting the heroes down, and a scientist studying how human DNA evolved to include these abilities in the first place.

Before going more off the rails in later seasons (and in a later spin-off, Heroes: Reborn , that couldn't quite recapture the magic), Heroes was a masterclass in complex storytelling. It's hard to imagine a broadcast network show quite as ambitious — or a version of this show that would have worked without Panettiere's performance.

How to watch: All four seasons of Heroes are available to stream on Netflix or for free with ads on Tubi .

That's the end of this week's episode, but there'll always be more TV to watch. I'll be back on Sept. 7 with new recommendations.

Think there's something missing that deserves my TV time? Let me know what else I should have on my radar in the comments below!

It's hard to imagine a broadcast network show quite as ambitious — or a version of this show that would have worked without Panettiere's performance.
How to watch: All four seasons of Heroes are available to stream on Netflix or for free with ads on Tubi .
That's the end of this week's episode, but there'll always be more TV to watch. I'll be back on Sept. 7 with new recommendations.
Think there's something missing that deserves my TV time? Let me know what else I should have on my radar in the comments below!

articles.title: Raspberry Pi shares its official tutorial for making a cyberdeck
articles.summary: Raspberry Pi is getting in on the viral cyberdeck trend with its own guide to building one of the homemade portable computers.
articles.body: Raspberry Pi’s head of social, Ashley Whittaker, acknowledged the cyberdeck trend today, saying “we haven’t been able to get away from cyberdecks this year.” Tiny portable computers made out of things like purses, jewelry boxes, and other thrifted or recycled parts have gone viral on TikTok and other social media platforms over the past year, and Raspberry Pi now has its own guide to building one of the homemade computers.  Raspberry Pi has also increased its prices multiple times this year due to rising costs for RAM and other components, which could be another reason to support this growing market of active and would-be hobbyists. The 16GB version of the Raspberry Pi 5 included in the company’s official cyberdeck guide got a $100 price hike in April, nearly as much as the board’s original $120 price. [Image: Raspberry Pi’s cyberdeck includes a Pi 5 board, Raspberry Pi flash drive, and a LiPo battery hidden under a Bluetooth keyboard. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/raspberry-pi-cyberdeck-inside.jpeg?quality=90&strip=all] Raspberry Pi’s cyberdeck guide includes a parts list and detailed assembly instructions, but sticks to a fairly simple design using a plain black Pelican-style case. As content creators are proving, though, you can make a cyberdeck out of just about anything. Annike Tan, whose cyberdecks have attracted millions of views on TikTok, continues to upgrade her “mermaid” purse cyberdeck with new design details and even added a USB hub. [Media: https://www.tiktok.com/@ubeboobey/video/7662053926086200598?is_from_webapp=1&sender_device=pc&web_id=7670279094521988639]

articles.title: 'Yellowstone' creator Taylor Sheridan sued by writer alleging he stole her idea
articles.summary: The hit drama, which ran for six years, is now the subject of a copyright lawsuit.
articles.body:
A writer is suing Yellowstone creator Taylor Sheridan, alleging he stole the idea for the show from a project she'd spent more than 10 years developing.

Lauren J. Salkin alleges that the hit drama series bears striking similarities to a script she pitched to Sheridan's team in 2016 and 2017, sharing "specific expressive choices," according to the lawsuit filed Friday and reviewed by TheWrap , Variety and the Independent . The suit also names 101 Studios, Paramount Global, NBCUniversal and other companies behind the show as defendants.

Yahoo News has reached out to Sheridan's representatives for comment.

Salkin says she submitted a completed pilot script for her own show, Sovereign Nation , along with a series bible and pitch deck, to Sheridan's representatives at Elevate Entertainment. The complaint describes Sovereign Nation as a "dramatic television series centered on tribal governance, casino-driven economic power and a modern war over land and development."

Yellowstone follows the Dutton family, owners of the largest ranch in Montana, as they navigate conflicts over land with developers, a neighboring Native American reservation and other parties.

Yellowstone ran for six years, from 2018 to 2024, becoming a massive hit for Paramount Network. Its star, Kevin Costner, won a Golden Globe for his role. The show has spawned four spinoffs; its latest, Dutton Ranch , was released in May. Three more spinoffs are in development.

Salkin's suit states that Sheridan's representatives told her he "thanks you very much for your interest," but "unfortunately, he's unavailable for TV projects," and that Paramount greenlighted Yellowstone just months later.

Salkin also says she met with a senior HBO executive who had reviewed her Sovereign Nation pitch. According to TheWrap 's account of the lawsuit, Salkin says the executive later told her HBO had rejected a Sheridan pitch for Yellowstone in spring 2017 because of its similarities to her work.

According to Variety , the suit states: "When the works are objectively compared, the same coordinated design repeatedly appears: casino-centered institutions organize political power; the same unusual land-development mechanisms propel the conflict; parallel scenes perform the same dramatic functions; and the same actors appear in materially parallel roles.

"These are not merely convergences of a shared genre. Taken together with access and timing, they support a strong inference of copying."

Speaking to Yahoo News, Salkin's attorney Paul B. Lackey said: "Obviously, it was not an easy decision for an individual screenwriter to decide to take on the titans of the entertainment industry.

"She has watched the exploitation of her hard work for too long and decided that enough was enough. We will now hold them accountable."

Salkin's lawyers also claim she suggested actors Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham, who appeared in Yellowstone , in her pitch deck.

Sheridan had worked with Birmingham on two films: Hell or High Water (2016) and Wind River , which was filmed in March and April 2016, several months before Salkin submitted her pitch to Elevate in late 2016 and early 2017.

Salkin is seeking an injunction against the continued use of her work, along with unspecified damages and profits tied to the alleged infringement. She has also requested a jury trial, according to HollywoodLife .

Sheridan has previously given his own account of the origins of Yellowstone . In 2023, he told the Hollywood Reporter that he pitched the project to HBO as a movie — The Godfather in Montana — before it evolved into the series that aired on Paramount Network.

articles.title: Mariska Hargitay's friends warned her not to host the Emmys. Then she decided it was worth the risk.
articles.summary: The "Law & Order: SVU" star explains why she ignored her friends' advice and took the gig — and how former "Colbert" writers are helping.
articles.body:
Mariska Hargitay is having an epic year.

The actor made her Broadway debut in the one-woman show Every Brilliant Thing this spring. Then in the summer, her beloved New York Knicks won their first NBA title in more than 50 years — she was courtside for their miraculous 29-point comeback in Game 4 of the NBA Finals. This fall, she's returning for her 28th (!) season of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit .

That's not all: In a few weeks, she'll host the Emmy Awards, becoming the first woman to do so in 15 years. My Mom Jayne , the HBO documentary she directed about her mother, Jayne Mansfield, is nominated for three awards.

When NBC and the Television Academy announced that she would host the Emmys, Hargitay said in a statement that it was a " great honor " for her to "celebrate this extraordinary community of storytellers."

But in a recent interview with Variety , Hargitay said that when NBC asked, she almost said no.

"At first I thought, 'This is ridiculously thankless — a difficult job that everyone gets ripped apart for. Why? Why would I do that?'" Hargitay recalled.

She said she then consulted with friends who had hosted awards shows, and they all told her the same thing: "Don't do it."

But her love for the medium, combined with a desire for new challenges, led her to go for it.

"I thought about why I love television," Hargitay said. "Television, in my opinion, is extraordinarily healing."

She's working with ex-'Late Show' writers

While Hargitay is the first non-comedian to host the Emmys since Angela Lansbury in 1993, she'll have some help.

In a recent interview with Deadline , Hargitay said that she's enlisted some of the writers from The Late Show With Stephen Colbert , which ended earlier this year, to help write her Emmys material.

"We're at the beginning stages, and so we're throwing out a lot of different ideas," she said. "I'm working with an incredible team of writers — the writers from Colbert … We've been meeting a lot and discussing a lot and pitching a lot of ideas. We're pitching so many ideas."

"I cannot tell you how many people — famous people — ask to be a dead body on the show. It's a thing," Hargitay said. "And it is so funny to me that that's what they want out of all the things … just to be a dead body. It's on their bucket list. That's one of the ideas that we were talking about."

Like several other New York-based stars , Hargitay is a diehard Knicks fan and has been a courtside fixture at their Madison Square Garden home games for years.

"And I'm a Knick!" she exclaimed at one point during her Variety interview.

She has become friends with point guard Jalen Brunson, who calls her "my favorite New York Knicks fan."

"I'm so grateful for the relationship we have been able to build over the last few years," Brunson told Variety. "As a lifelong fan of 'SVU,' her support means the world to me. I'm truly grateful to have her in my corner."

Brunson also attended the New York premiere of My Mom Jayne and a performance of Every Brilliant Thing , the Broadway show that Hargitay starred in during the Knicks' championship run.

Hargitay told Variety that she half-jokingly asked to have the night off to watch the Knicks' title-clinching Game 5, which was played in San Antonio. She said she watched the second half from home.

"My heart was in two places — I'm not going to lie," she said.

On the night of Game 4, Hargitay said she shortened her performance so she could make it in time for tip-off.

"I need to be there. I need this for them!" she said. Hargitay sat in the first row next to Taylor Swift and Alana Haim, each of whom wore custom Knicks T-shirts. (Hargitay's said, "Stevie Knicks.")

After the team's improbable 29-point comeback, she was seen on the floor of the Garden with her mouth open, seemingly stunned by what she had just witnessed.

"You're standing in a miracle," Hargitay said. "The world was changed. New York was changed. The bar of what's possible has changed. You can be down 29 points and still win — this is what's in the consciousness of young athletes now."

When a reporter asked Brunson what was next for him after his team won the championship, he said, " Try and get on SVU ." Hargitay confirmed that "it's definitely happening" in a recent interview .

"He's kind of magnificent that way," she said. "He is just open and ready. I don't think there is much Jalen can't do."

Hargitay, who won an Emmy in 2006 for her work on Law & Order: SVU , could win another — while she's hosting the show. Her HBO documentary, My Mom Jayne , has been nominated for three Emmys, including Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special and Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program.

The film is about her mother, Jayne Mansfield, who died in a car accident outside New Orleans in 1967. Hargitay and her two older brothers, Zoltán and Miklos, were in the back seat of the vehicle but survived.

In interviews, she has described the documentary as "an archaeological dig" about the generational trauma her family experienced.

"I had no idea how it would be received, so it's been extraordinary to see how it's resonated with people," Hargitay said recently on NBC's Today show . "And that has been the biggest gift of all."

articles.title: Android is getting its own weird dots to cure car sickness
articles.summary: Google’s Motion Assist taps into your device’s accelerometer and gyroscope to place dots around the periphery of the display that move in harmony with the car.
articles.body: Google is rolling out a new Android feature that’s been proven to reduce, or even eliminate, motion sickness when using a phone inside a moving vehicle. Dubbed Motion Assist by Google, it’s very similar to Apple’s Motion Cues, first introduced in 2024. The Android 17 feature appears to be rolling out in phases, with some Pixel phones getting it first, according to Android Authority. The science behind these magic dots is sound, and addresses the motion sickness felt when staring at a static display while the inner ear feels the car turning, braking, and accelerating. Motion Assist taps into your device’s accelerometer and gyroscope to place dots around the periphery of the display that move in harmony with the motion of the car. When the car turns right, the dots sweep across the screen to the left; when the car brakes, the dots slide forward. [Image: Here’s how it works on Apple devices. https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/motion-dots.gif?quality=90&strip=all] I’m here to tell you that this tech really works. As an avid vanlifer, I’m often working on my MacBook and iPhone from the passenger seat while we drive to the next destination. But that’s only possible by activating the anti-nausea feature, otherwise I can’t stomach it. My wife is a convert, too. Google lets you set the opacity of the motion indicators and choose from a variety of shapes and colors. The feature can be configured to turn on automatically when it detects a moving vehicle, or it can be quickly toggled through a tile in your Quick Settings. The feature hasn’t arrived yet on a pair of Pixel devices we tested. But if you’re lucky, you’ll find Motion Assist in your Google Settings under Your Profile and All Services.

articles.title: Greenworks’ MaximusZ electric riding mower has five motors and a few compromises
articles.summary: Greenworks’ MaximusZ electric riding mower is more than a mower — which it had better be, given the price.
articles.body: The current EV market is flush with variety. I’ve driven single-motor economy-minded machines, dual-motor EVs with all-wheel drive, tri-motor vehicles that dial up the performance stakes, and even wild quad-motor performance cars, like the Rimac Nevera. But this is the first time I’ve ever driven a five-motor EV, one with the agility and speed to turn a 360 even more smoothly than an electric G-Wagon. It also makes quick work of terrible turf. This is, of course, a lawn mower, and it only uses two of those motors to drive the wheels. The other three turn a trio of blades that cut a 54-inch-wide swath in a single pass. It also promises four acres on a charge and is positioned as the ultimate mowing machine. For $8,799, it had better be. For a company that spent much of its life building white-label tools for other brands, Changzhou, China-based Greenworks has quickly leaped to the forefront of battery-powered products for those trying to phase out internal combustion in every facet of their lives. Opening a manufacturing facility in Tennessee in 2023 certainly helped elevate its domestic cred.  The company offers a wide portfolio of products from power tools to go-karts energized by a dizzying array of often incompatible battery technologies. The 80-volt architecture within the MaximusZ mower here is the company’s latest, with Greenworks offering various packs of various sizes. This mower uses four smaller 6.0Ah and two large, 17-pound 16Ah packs to offer a combined battery capacity of 56Ah. That, Greenworks says, is enough to do four acres on a single charge.  [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/2026-Greenworks-MaximusZ-014.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/2026-Greenworks-MaximusZ-016.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/2026-Greenworks-MaximusZ-019.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/2026-Greenworks-MaximusZ-021.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/2026-Greenworks-MaximusZ-022.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] [Image: https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/08/2026-Greenworks-MaximusZ-023.jpg?quality=90&strip=all] Charging duties are handled by a disappointingly proprietary charger. I greatly wish Greenworks engineered this thing to work with a standard SAE J1772 plug, or even NACS, but it is quick at least, with Greenworks estimating a full charge at 3.5 hours. At nearly $9,000, the MaximusZ’s cost may seem extreme, but in this space it’s actually competitive. With a maximum speed of 8mph and 41 horsepower on tap, it’s comparable to something like a Stihl RZ 552, which retails for $9,499. It even out-powers some professional-grade machines, like a $18,899 Toro 6000 Series. But is it truly comparable?  It has a few key advantages, the biggest of course being its relative lack of noise and vibration. Not burning gas is an increasingly big deal, too, as is a lack of carburetors to clean and oils to change. Finally, the MaximusZ features a little dumper bed on the back and even a tow hitch.  All those reasons are why I decided to bring one home, but before I could start flaying the fescue, I had to pick a mowing height. That’s easy in the MaximusZ. A pedal on the right lifts the entire mower deck, while a grid defines its height in quarter-inch increments. Step on the pedal, put the pin in the right hole, then take your foot off the pedal, and you’re good to go. It’s almost crude in its simplicity, but it works well.  Next was figuring out the controls. Twist the key and the mower takes about eight seconds to boot up. That’s just long enough to be annoying. Above the key there’s a dim, 4.0-inch LCD that picks up a new scratch every time you look at it too hard. Squint, though, and you can see the current state of charge, maximum mower speed, maximum blade speed, and total runtime.  The buttons under the display let you toggle the blade and mower speeds or enter a menu to change a scant few settings. That 1.5 acres of mowable land I have is split up across a half-dozen small patches, plus a larger pasture, which means I had ample opportunity to test both the MaximusZ’s agility and its stability. I started in the slowest mode until I got the hang of things, which caps you at roughly half the thing’s maximum cutting speed of 8mph. You steer the mower with the two handles. Push them apart from each other, and the mower goes into a sort of park mode. Pull them inward, and the motors are engaged. Each handle controls the corresponding motor on that side, so pushing the right handle all the way forward has the mower turning to the left. Pull the left handle toward you at the same time, and it’ll spin on its own axis. Quite abruptly, if you’re not smooth. That, though, is the only suspension on the machine, making this a rough ride over tree roots and the like. There are integrated USB-A and USB-C ports, a slot for your smartphone, and two cupholders.  And what about noise? I measured 85dB at maximum blade speed, significantly lower than the 90 to 100dB of a commercial-grade mower. That may not sound like much, but a 10dB increase equates to a 10x increase in acoustic force. While you can safely listen to 85dB for eight hours without concern, at 95dB, you can damage your hearing in just 60 minutes. I still wear earplugs to be safe, but I appreciate the relative quiet and lack of harsh vibrations. When the blades are stopped and I’m zipping up and down the driveway, it’s silent and smooth.  At its fastest speed, with the blades on maximum, I can mow my entire property in slightly over one hour. I’ve now done that three times, each time consuming roughly 75 percent of the mower’s battery capacity. Doing the math, that means two acres could be possible at maximum speed. That’s short of the promised four acres, but again, I have a lot of small, oddly shaped patches to mow, and I’m doing it at top speed. Were I mowing at lower speeds, and if I had a single, large pasture, three acres seems like a safe bet without pausing for a recharge or battery swap. That advertised figure of four, though, feels optimistic. The mower has an annoying tendency to drain the four smaller batteries before tapping into the bigger packs. I fear the extra charging cycles these smaller packs face mean they’ll wear out more quickly than if the larger packs were depleted first.  And as far as charging goes, Greenworks’ estimate of 3.5 hours seem fair. articles.title: Fitbit founders launch Luffu Link, an LTE health and safety band | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Luffu Link combines all-day health sensing, voice logging, location awareness, and the ability to get help from trusted contacts into a single device, all without needing a phone nearby.
articles.body:
Luffu , a new startup from Fitbit’s co-founders James Park and Eric Friedman, on Tuesday launched Luffu Link, an LTE-enabled health and safety band designed to monitor the wearer’s overall health, both physical and mental. The wearable combines all-day health sensing, voice logging, location awareness, and the ability to get help from trusted contacts into a single device, even when no phone is nearby.

The currently $250 device is available for preorder and is expected to ship in early 2027. It comes in three colors: halo gold, onyx black, and sterling blue.

Luffu Link represents the next step in the startup’s mission to develop an intelligent family care system, as it complements the Luffu health-monitoring app , launched earlier this year. The app uses AI in the background to gather and organize family information, learn day-to-day patterns, and flag notable changes so families can stay aligned and address potential well-being issues.

Luffu was born out of Park and Friedman’s own experiences caring for their families and aging parents. They built Luffu to give families a clearer picture of a loved one’s health without constant check-ins or making them feel monitored.

“When you become a family caregiver, or the CEO of the family, these people are spending an enormous amount of time doing it,” Park said in an interview with TechCrunch. “Research shows over 27 hours a week on average, which is a crazy amount of time…I think technology can play a big role in helping reduce this load, but as we found out, the tools to help them are pretty fragmented,” he said.

Link users can press a button to capture information in the moment by voice, like updates about medications, symptoms, meals, mood, reminders, and more. The Luffu app then organizes that information and incorporates it into the family’s broader context. The company sees its market as including family caregivers, independent older adults, and health- and safety-conscious adults who want to stay on top of their health.

The wearable also continuously collects standard health and wellness data, such as activity, sleep, resting heart rate, calories burned, heart-rate variability (HRV), and breathing rate to identify daily patterns, track changes over time, and provide personalized insights or alerts.

“Link does a lot of what a typical health tracker would do, but it’s not just about tracking,” Park said. “It’s about what Luffu does with that data. It’s looking for patterns, so maybe your activity has been unusually low,” he continues.

“Maybe your sleep patterns have changed. Maybe that change happened after a new medication. So it’s looking at all this data, and it’s not to give families another dashboard full of graphs — I designed a lot of that at Fitbit — it’s to help answer some key questions like ‘what changed? Does it matter? Does somebody need to know?’ And people can just continue to live their life without feeling like they’re being constantly monitored.”

The device uses built-in GPS to keep trusted contacts informed of a wearer’s location, including where they have been and when they enter or leave specific areas. A quick double press also lets the wearer check in with family members without making a call or sending a text. Additionally, built-in LTE lets wearers send a help request without needing to use a phone. (The LTE data service is included so it doesn’t require a separate carrier plan.)

For example, the wearer could press the button and say something like, “I fell and hurt my wrist. Can someone come get me?” Link will then send the voice message along with the wearer’s location, battery level, and health data, like their heart rate and recent activity, to trusted family members.

Unlike other screenless wearables on the market that are focused on individual health and fitness, Link is designed around everyday health and family connection, the company says.

“There’s a trend to have no screens on this new class of wearables, but here, it’s very purposeful,” Park explained. “We want to be in the background. Link is designed to be on your wrist as a quiet guardian throughout your day, and we also wanted to make this feel nothing like a traditional wearable, nothing like a generic-looking fabric brand or a wrist thing with a screen or a bulky pendant that you’re wearing for emergency purposes. So, the device takes a lot of cues from jewelry.”

The startup teased that it’s developing a home device that extends Luffu into the home, marking the next step in its intelligent family care system.

While Link is currently available for preorder at a discounted price, its expected retail price is $300.
